properties.name: Corroboration reads as corroboration

properties.description: Turn a gap into a question in the user's words.
properties.name: Ask the user a plain question

properties.description: BUILT 2026-07-25 as the `find_tools` tool. Imported from github-mcp-server's pkg/tooldiscovery, which fuzzy-searches its own tool list with weighted scoring and returns three results by default. reflow2 serves 97 tools, and req:agent-native's promise — every capability reachable from a coding agent over one surface — is only true in principle if the agent can find the tool: a surface too large to hold in context is reachable the way a library with no catalogue is readable. Scored over `tool_router.list_all()`, the served surface itself, so the catalogue cannot drift from the tools that exist — the failure mode skill_lint exists to catch in prose, avoided here by construction rather than by a second list. Weights follow the source: an exact name outranks a name substring, which outranks a description hit, which outranks a parameter-name hit. Ties break by name so the same query answers the same way twice, because a ranking that reshuffles teaches an agent not to trust it. Summaries come back trimmed to the first sentence — a catalogue that costs as much to read as the surface it indexes is pointless — and the result names `matched`, `omitted` and `searched`, so a query that found nothing says so instead of falling back to the whole list.
properties.name: Find the right tool on a surface too large to hold in context

properties.description: Extends the confirmation ledger (cap:freshness) with the verification side of the same question. Per capability: the newest dated last_run_at across its passing VERIFIES checks, set beside the dates the ledger already computes for baseline accepts on its realizing artifacts — so a reader can see that a capability is claiming `verified` on a check that predates the code it covers. A SIGNAL, NOT A GAP, deliberately (dec:verification-freshness-not-a-gap): it is a standing property of the claim rather than an event, it fires on every legitimate refactor as readily as on a real hole, and a list that can never reach zero gets skimmed — which is the failure the whole gap workflow exists to prevent. THREE CONSTRAINTS THE CORE ALREADY IMPOSES AND THIS MUST HONOUR: the core takes no clock, so this compares recorded timestamps supplied by callers and never asks the system what time it is; undated events are not comparable, which the ledger already states; and where either side is undated the answer is an explicit `unknown` that is REPORTED, never a silent pass — an unanswerable freshness question presented as freshness is the same lie in a new place.
properties.name: Say whether a check is older than what it checks

properties.description: Tell a client what types exist and what may join them.
properties.name: Describe the vocabulary

properties.description: The answer to "what is the most pressing item?" once the backlog lives in the graph. It is NOT detect_gaps and NOT check-health, and the distinction is the design: detect_gaps asks what the design has not yet decided, check-health asks what shape is wrong, and this asks which of the agreed things to do now. Three different questions needing three different actions, often from three different people. Composed rather than invented — BL-85 already specifies the form ("a backlog_report / roadmap projection, a view, never a second source of truth"), BL-68 supplies readiness and risk-to-completion ("the roadmap is a risk-burndown schedule"), BL-40 is the projection layer, and the long narratives stay as documents-linked artifacts rather than being crushed into properties. THE RANKING RULE THAT MATTERS MOST: an unmade decision outranks the work waiting on it. A proposed Decision with things GOVERNED_BY it is a blocker, and pointing someone at blocked work is worse than saying nothing, because it looks like progress. Measured 2026-07-24, this is not hypothetical: dec:multi-writer-architecture blocks two nodes, so the honest answer to "what is next" right now is a decision only the human can make, not a build task. PREREQUISITE, and the reason this cannot usefully ship first: today ZERO accepted requirements lack a satisfying capability, so "what is unbuilt" is unanswerable from the graph — everything accepted is allocated to something. Distinguishing allocated from delivered needs cap:derived-completion (BL-104). Until that lands, this view can rank what is undecided and what is misshapen but is blind to what is merely unfinished. PLANNED.
properties.name: Say what to work on next, as a projection with its reasoning shown

alternatives
properties.purpose: The fork module: analysis of alternatives across branch exports, the decision point (a proposed Decision holding forkable siblings), its collapse into a winner plus retired losers, and — planned — the fork point that resolves a past Decision to the design it was made against.

properties.name: claims
properties.purpose: The coordination module: who has which region of the design in hand, and where two people are working the same ground. Advisory only — it holds no locks and refuses no writes, because the design lives as a file in each checkout with no shared server to hold one (dec:multi-writer-architecture). Regions are computed from a seed and a depth via the same traversal propagate_from uses, so they follow the design rather than freezing a membership list.

properties.name: degraded
properties.purpose: The server that starts when the graph cannot be opened: one tool, reflow2_unavailable, and the reason in the handshake instructions.

properties.name: docs
properties.purpose: The human-facing documents: the README that says what reflow2 is and how it runs, the getting-started material that installs and connects it, and the diagrams. Distinct from the skills, which instruct the agent, and from the questions the Human Channel asks — this is what a person reads before they are a user, and possibly before they are convinced.

properties.name: identity
properties.purpose: Which design this store holds: minting, adoption, refusal, and the label on top.

properties.name: merge
properties.purpose: The three-way merge module: the typed-node case table against a common ancestor, conflict minting as Questions, resolution into a merged design, atomic apply, and rerere resolution memory. Compare's sibling — compare says how two records differ, merge says what to do about it.

properties.name: nudge
properties.purpose: Whether this project's session-end nudge exists, and saying so when it does not.

properties.name: sanitize
properties.purpose: The ingress trust boundary: the one place that neutralises instruction-carrying characters in text arriving from outside the session, and reports what it stripped. Deliberately a separate module rather than a helper inside ingest, because the same boundary has to serve graph import and, later, any hosted surface — a filter that lives inside one caller is a filter the next caller forgets.

properties.name: scope
properties.purpose: Scoped analysis: the region a part of the design covers (containment closure, then traceability radius) and the detectors narrowed to it, with the four buckets that keep a narrowed answer honest. Separate from cmp:detect because the question is different — detect decides what a finding IS, this decides whose it is.

properties.name: skills
properties.purpose: The served skill catalogue: embedded bodies, the instruction catalogue, and the two tools that read them.

properties.name: sync
properties.purpose: The judgement about writing over a shared design record: what would be lost, said in the language of what to do about it.

properties.name: Agent Surface
properties.purpose: The boundary the agent lives behind: the reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio, and the consumer kit that installs it.

properties.name: Coherence Loop
properties.purpose: The engine: on any change, find the ripples and surface them — detect gaps, propagate impact, heal structure, reconcile against what was built, proven and deployed, and report where the design stands.

properties.name: Documentation
properties.purpose: The explanation reflow2 ships with itself. Modelled as a subsystem of the product rather than as material about the product, on the user's call (2026-07-24): documentation is part of any deliverable, and a system handed over without it has not been fully delivered — his analogy was designing a fighter jet in reflow2 and shipping no documentation to the people who must operate it. The consequence taken seriously here is that documentation gets the same treatment as code: its files are registered Artifacts with checksums, so a README that drifts away from what the system does is a detectable defect rather than a thing someone eventually notices.

properties.name: Human Channel
properties.purpose: Turn an underspecified design into a plain-language question for the human, and remember what was asked.

properties.name: Intake
properties.purpose: The front door: bring intent into the graph, greenfield (genesis from a brief) or brownfield (adopt/ingest from an existing system).

properties.name: Design Store
properties.purpose: Durable, deterministic memory: the schema-validated graph that persists in the project, exports and imports byte-identically, is searchable, and stamps which reflow2 wrote it.

properties.name: Time & History
properties.purpose: The change axis: epochs, decisions, the roads not taken — hold and compare alternatives, diff and merge divergent designs, so the past survives being updated.

properties.name: Vocabulary
properties.purpose: The neutral type system — the node and edge types that ARE a design. What any design is made of, before any of it is stored or checked.

properties.name: Pairing sees boundaries, not the types that cross them
properties.statement:
A HARD LIMIT ON WHAT `req:complementary-pairing` CAN EVER CATCH, found by the dynograph-foundation trial on 2026-07-28 and not by review.

THE CASE, verified from both sides. dynograph-foundation's `ifc:storage-api` exposes `search_fulltext`, whose signature returns `Vec<dynograph_text::TextHit>`. reflow2 consumes that call and reads all three of the struct's public fields — `node_id`, `node_type`, `score` (`crates/reflow2-core/src/search.rs:67-79`). So reflow2 structurally depends on a type belonging to `dynograph-text`, a crate it NEVER NAMES as a dependency, through a boundary belonging to `dynograph-storage`. Two separately published boundaries are entangled by a type that crosses one of them, and the offer document says they are separate.

WHY PAIRING CANNOT SEE IT. Every axis in the pairing key is a property OF A BOUNDARY: `medium`, `transport_security`, `auth`, the name, the payload format. This seam agrees on all of them. Provider publishes a `library` boundary, consumer requires a `library` boundary, both `unspecified` on transport and auth because a linked crate has neither — the match is clean and correct at every level the rule inspects. The break lives one layer down, in a struct's field list, which no boundary property mentions. A change to `TextHit` breaks a consumer that no document either side holds would predict.

THE GENERAL FORM: a type that crosses a boundary is part of the contract, and the offer models boundaries, not types. `payload_format` says `json` and not which fields; `payload_schema` can point at a schema for a wire format, but nothing does the equivalent for a linked-library signature, where the "wire" is the type system itself.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PAIRING RULE — this is what makes it a constraint rather than a to-do. Pairing must NOT report a clean match as evidence of compatibility. It can honestly say "these two boundaries can be connected"; it cannot say "and nothing crossing them will break you". Those are different claims, and conflating them rebuilds the false green the same trial already produced once. The pairing report should say what it did not examine, the way `coverage_report` says what it never heard of.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE IT, noted so the constraint is not mistaken for permanent: comparing the TYPES that cross a boundary, not just the boundary. For a library seam that is signature and struct-shape comparison — real work, language-specific, and nothing reflow2 does today is close to it. For a wire seam `payload_schema` already points at the answer if both sides fill it in. Until one of those exists, this limit stands and must be STATED rather than discovered.

TWO SMALLER LESSONS FROM THE SAME FINDING. First, the counterparty found it, not the owner of either half — reflow2 could not see that its own `cmp:search` edge pointed at the wrong boundary, and dynograph could not see that its type had escaped. Second, both sides had over-attributed a DIFFERENT risk (`TextError::ReadOnly`) in opposite directions for a day, because both were reasoning about the type and neither had read the call: `search_fulltext` flattens `TextError` to a string, so it never crosses at all. The type that crosses is the one that matters, and only the signature says which that is.

properties.decision: Take a claim when you need one and start — but publish it by pushing it, every time, not only when contested; a claim nobody can see is not a claim. When two claims cross, the winner is whichever landed first in git history, and both parties can verify that independently. Rejected: a coordination service or lock manager (contradicts dec:multi-writer-architecture, and single-writer exclusion is the observed failure), and asking before every claim (the fleet measured that timidity starves the pool).
properties.name: Seats coordinate by announcement and provable order, never by exclusion
properties.rationale: The StoryFlow fleet runs 15+ concurrent seats on exactly this rule — grab-and-go, announce always, crossings settled "first-on-disk, both provable". reflow2 has better material for the provable half than a markdown timestamp: a content-hash chain and git order. The alternative people reach for by reflex is a lock, and a lock is exactly what took five of six sessions offline on 2026-07-25.

properties.decision:
EPIGRAPH — "Two roads diverged in a wood, and I— / I took the one less traveled by, / And that has made all the difference." — Robert Frost, 'The Road Not Taken'. Aptly, the poem is itself a hindsight tale: the speaker concedes the two roads were worn 'really about the same' and foresees telling it 'with a sigh' ages hence — the difference is authored in retrospect, not known at the fork. That is this decision's whole bet: credit for a road taken is assigned in hindsight, by the human, never scored in advance. (Unofficially, 'the Robert Frost decision.')

reflow2 holds every Decision's alternatives as UNRANKED, forkable siblings — not a scored trade-study runner-up. The design is modelled as a navigable decision-MDP: the graph is the world-model (propagate/detect/compare evaluate a fork's consequences before anything is built), branches are the replay, and the reward signal is two-channel — the structural detectors (in-model holes: SPOFs, cycles, gaps) plus field trials (out-of-model holes only a real episode reveals, e.g. BL-74's loop-on-virtue collapse). Alternatives are stored cheaply (the unchosen option + its rationale, at the decision's epoch) and their consequence design is COMPUTED on demand by forking that epoch and replaying — never eagerly maintained as N full parallel designs, which would combinatorially explode and rot as the main line moves on (a non-stationary design). Which fork to expand is chosen by where the surprise is — a fresh defect, a failed trial, or a rationale that already flags doubt points back to a decision (high 'TD error') — not by enumerating the whole tree. Crucially the human is the reward function and does the credit assignment and policy update; reflow2 supplies the replay buffer and the world-model but never auto-optimizes a design by replay-and-score.
properties.name: Alternatives are unranked forkable siblings; the human judges in hindsight, not a stored score
properties.rationale: User decided the ranked-vs-unranked scope 2026-07-22 after developing the idea across three framings — choose-your-own-adventure (the decision tree you can turn back to), Analysis of Alternatives (the runner-up kept live), and a reinforcement-learning gridworld (replay an episode until you cross without falling in a hole). Unranked over a scored AoA because reflow2 routes judgment to the human (dec:report-dont-judge, dec:three-party-checks): a stored ranking would be the system asserting a preference it cannot honestly hold, and design episodes are too few, too expensive and too subjective for a stationary reward anyway. Derived-over-stored (store the fork, compute the consequence) is reflow2's recurring lesson (dec:certainty-derived, dec:component-verified-computed) and the only defence against an eagerly-maintained alternative rotting under a moving main line. Model-based-planning-not-model-free-crashing is the whole point of a design brain: propagate_change computes the blast radius before you edit, so you simulate the hole instead of falling in it — but BL-74 proves some holes are out-of-model and only a field episode finds them. This unifies the branch (BL-70), merge (dec:merge-three-way / dec:merge-conflict-semantics — how a forked road comes home) and claims (BL-44) threads under one primitive: alternatives as first-class, forkable, comparable, mergeable. The hindsight pass that motivated it is the mechanism already working by hand — dec:merge-survivor-provenance carries a 'reconsider' note tracing a near-bad merge back to its own fork. Deferred to their own decisions: how an alternative attaches to a Decision in the schema, the fork/branch ref layer (BL-70), the 'when has an episode taught us enough to revise' trigger, and the tool surface.

properties.decision: detect_gaps sorts anchored gaps before project-level phase nudges, severity within each band.
properties.name: A gap that names nodes outranks a phase nudge
properties.rationale: A named gap says something is wrong NOW; a nudge says what comes next. Ranking 'next' above 'broken' made three brownfield trials do the useless thing first. Nudges are demoted, never suppressed. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); evidence: gap-surfacing disciplines 3 and 8.

properties.decision: possible_duplicate is a DETECT gap; HEAL merges only on a human-drawn DUPLICATES edge.
properties.name: Suspected duplicates are asked, never merged
properties.rationale: apply_heal deletes a node with no undo, so merge is safe only because the endpoints were asserted; a heuristic must not drive it. A gap can be acknowledged, a HEAL defect cannot be dismissed. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); evidence: 3dtictactoe trial, BL-27/BL-29.

properties.decision: reflow2's own decomposition is the seven functional systems a design-graph tool IS — vocabulary, store, coherence-loop, human-channel, time-history, intake, agent-surface — with the 38 Rust modules re-parented under them as implementation. The as-built crate grouping (reflow2-core / -mcp / kit) is retired from the as-designed view.
properties.name: reflow2's systems are functional, not its file tree
properties.rationale: The self-model had been recovered backwards from the file tree, so its 38 Components were the Rust module list and the domain primitives a design-graph product fundamentally is — node and edge types — appeared nowhere (BL-83). A functional carving comes from the product's purpose (a genesis input), not the code, and cuts across crate boundaries, so adopt on the code can only re-derive the module view. Derived with the user, 2026-07-23. The retired crate view is recovered by adopt-on-a-copy (BL-83b) and the divergence measured by compare_designs (BL-83c).

properties.decision: UNDECIDED. Raised by Anthony 2026-07-25 from his own situation: he is in Long Island, his brother is in Washington State, they want to work on one design at the same time and to see each other's projects. FOUR ROADS, and the middle ones are not the obvious winners. (a) GIT IS ALREADY THE CENTRAL SERVER — the design is a file in the repo, the repo already spans both coasts, and the claims layer that shipped 2026-07-25 already answers "who has what in hand" the moment either side pulls. Nothing to host, nothing to secure, nothing to pay for, and no new place for the design to live. What it cannot do is tell you about a claim before the other person pushes. (b) A HOSTED MCP over HTTPS — one server process holding the graph, both people's agents connecting to it, so a claim is visible the moment it is made and a design is reachable by someone who never cloned the repo. Costs: reflow2-mcp serves stdio only today (rmcp's streamable-HTTP transport exists, the binary does not use it), authentication does not exist at all, and it puts the design on a machine — which weakens but does not erase dec:repo-file-embedded's objection, since the machine would be Anthony's own droplet rather than a vendor's. NOTE WHAT MAKES (b) CHEAPER THAN IT LOOKS: one server process with many clients is ALREADY compatible with the single-writer store, because there is still exactly one writer — the server. (c) HYBRID — host a read/publish surface for reaching and browsing designs, keep writes local and merge through git, so the durable record never moves. THE CHEAPEST FIRST CUT, worth naming because it needs almost no core work: one server process PER PROJECT, each with its own graph path and its own token, and project selection becomes which URL the agent points at — no graph_id plumbing, no multi-tenancy, and a per-project blast radius if one goes wrong. A private tailnet instead of public TLS removes the authentication problem for exactly two people, which is the population this actually has. (d) ONE LIVE SHARED WORKING TREE on a droplet — both people editing the same checkout simultaneously, seeing each other's edits, with a push to a "true" git repo every so often for permanent storage (Anthony, 2026-07-25). THE DESIGN HALF OF THIS IS (b) AND IS SOUND; THE CODE HALF INVERTS THE PROPERTY IT IS REACHING FOR. A shared checkout does not remove conflicts, it removes conflict DETECTION: with one copy there is no common ancestor to merge against, so two agents doing read-modify-write on one file interleave into last-write-wins with no marker, no three-way merge and nothing to review — strictly less safe than what they have now. It also shares the things git assumes are private (one index, one HEAD, one branch: `git checkout` on his side changes files under her mid-edit), shares the build directory and the graph's single-writer lock, and makes the droplet a single point of failure for two people who can currently both work on a plane. The batched push is its own cost: history granularity, attribution and bisect all collapse into one commit, the gates that are supposed to gate a commit are replaced by a timer, and "every so often" is precisely the size of the loss window when the droplet dies.
properties.name: OPEN — does reflow2 gain a hosted surface (one MCP over HTTPS) alongside the repo file?
properties.rationale: Held proposed, not built, because it sits against a decision made HOURS earlier on 2026-07-25 (dec:multi-writer-architecture: repo file plus merge on pull, no hosted service) and it must not be drifted into. Per dec:reopen-supersedes, the move is a NEW decision point rather than flipping that one back to proposed. What is genuinely new, and the reason this is not a rerun of the same argument: that decision answered "how do two writers avoid clobbering each other", and its rationale turned on concurrency being hypothetical and on not putting the user's design on someone else's machine. Neither objection addresses what was raised now — two machines that never share a filesystem, several projects per person, and wanting to READ and contribute to a design without cloning its repo. It is also the second field-sourced trigger in two days on the same seam, which is what cap:revise-trigger exists to notice; that it arrived by conversation rather than by detector is a finding about the detector, not about the trigger. THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded so nobody has to rediscover it: reflow2's loop is ask-the-human-and-record-the-decision, which is deliberate, attributable and slow — a shared live server optimises for simultaneity, which this tool does not need and may be harmed by. The thing the two of them described wanting is mostly non-colliding parallel work plus visibility, and git plus the claims layer already delivers most of that. What it does NOT deliver is the publishing case, and that is the strongest argument on the hosted side. WHAT OPTION (d) CLARIFIED, and it is the useful split: the appeal is real-time VISIBILITY, and visibility does not require a shared working tree. The graph is the artefact where simultaneity genuinely pays and where a single writer already exists to serialise it; source code is the artefact where the distributed copy is doing load-bearing work that a shared tree would silently undo. So the two halves of "host it" should be decided separately rather than together.

properties.decision: Requirement certainty is a computed reading, never a stored third axis: status accepted/met → user-confirmed; status deferred/dropped → settled out (also the user's word); status proposed → asserted (provenance authored/planned/imported) or recovered (provenance inferred/reconciled/healed). The load-bearing doctrine: an agent captures requirements at proposed and ONLY the user's answer moves the status — accepted, met, deferred and dropped are all user-only verbs. Reports render the certainty breakdown directly so no session reconstructs it in prose.
properties.name: A Requirement's certainty is derived from status × provenance; every move off proposed is the user's word
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22 (BL-75 vocabulary session, from their fleet trial: where-am-i had to caveat user-confirmed vs recovered in prose every session). Derived over stored for the BL-73 reason — a third stored property can contradict the two axes that already span the space, and the backlog's own warning was 'decide deliberately, not additively'. Every-move-off-proposed rather than accepted-only because an agent dropping a requirement on its own judgment is exactly the silent decision the loop exists to prevent — and this is BL-12 sketch idea 2's example made real ('a requirement moves to accepted only on the human's say-so'), enforced culturally in the skills and the tool description today; the mechanical half stays with BL-41. 'Recovered' over the trial's 'adopted' because it matches the graph's own vocabulary (cap:adopt: 'Recover a design from an existing system') and names the fact, not the workflow. No schema change: the whole defect was the read side — the second time this week (BL-73) the vocabulary was already sufficient and unread.

properties.decision: The eight slash commands (`/gaps`, `/health`, `/where`, `/req`, `/decisions`, `/debt`, `/brainstorm`, `/kpp`) are INSTALLED into a consumer project's `.claude/commands/`. Skills, working instructions and everything else remain SERVED. Anthony's call, 2026-07-28.
properties.name: Slash commands ship with the kit — the one narrow exception to serving everything
properties.rationale:
QUALIFIES `dec:skills-served` rather than overturning it, and the distinction is what makes the exception safe.

WHY THAT DECISION EXISTS: a copied skill goes stale, and the agent then loads last release's content in preference to what the server would serve. That happened here for four releases running without anything noticing, which is why nothing is copied.

WHY A COMMAND IS DIFFERENT: each is four lines that name a skill and say how to report the answer. There is no version-coupled content in it. When the skill behind it changes, the command is still correct, because the skill is fetched fresh at use time — the command is a pointer, and the thing it points at is the thing that moves.

THE ONE WAY IT CAN ROT, and it is now closed: a command could name a skill that no longer exists. `skill_lint` fails on exactly that, so the failure is caught in this repo rather than discovered in a consumer's, where the symptom would be an agent reporting it cannot find a skill the user was told to use. The mirror is byte-checked too, so `.claude/commands` cannot drift from the kit source.

WHAT IT COSTS IF WE ARE WRONG: eight small files in a consumer repo, each independently deletable, none of which changes behaviour when stale. Compare the cost of a stale skill, which silently answers with last release's method.

WHY IT WAS WORTH DOING AT ALL: without them a consumer install is experienced as BROKEN rather than thin — the skills are reachable and nothing tells you they are. That is the same invisibility `req:kit-reaches-the-agent` was raised for, one layer up: the pointer now reaches the agent, and the commands are what make the reachable thing usable.

properties.decision: A capability's verification state is three-valued: verified (a passing check of its own), component_verified (no check of its own, but a component it is allocated to carries a passing one — computed at read time, never written), and unchecked. The coverage line reports the third state as its own clause; detect_gaps replaces the N per-capability unverified alarms with ONE component_granularity_verification gap per carrying component at 0.35 — listing the riding capabilities, acknowledgeable once; status_contradiction accepts component-granularity proof for a verified status claim; loop_status counts component_verified as proven. A failing component suite carries nothing: passing-is-verified holds at every granularity.
properties.name: Component-granularity verification is a computed third state, one question per component
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22 (BL-73 vocabulary session, from their own fleet's field trial): a brownfield adopt with real per-service suites plus a 137-file integration suite read as '0/20 capabilities verified' and cost 21 near-identical acknowledge writes. Computed state over a bulk-attest write because the graph should record exactly what was checked — the component — and derive what that means one hop away; manufactured capability-level VERIFIES edges would be indistinguishable from direct checks forever after. The word component_verified because it says where the check lives. One gap per component because the residual question ('is component granularity enough for these?') is genuinely per-component and deserves to be asked once, not N times — the BL-42 lesson again: a loud detector needs a different question, not a tuned number. The write side needed nothing: VERIFIES accepts any target and even carries an unused coverage enum — the whole defect was the read side.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED, and recorded as BRAINSTORMING rather than as a proposal — Anthony's own framing, 2026-07-25, thinking out loud. His starting doubt is the right one and had not been written down: claiming a cluster of nodes says nothing about the REPOSITORY, and if the design and the code share one repo, two people working different clusters still collide in git even when they never touch the same node. FOUR IDEAS AS HE PUT THEM. (1) reflow2 REPLACES git — the graph defines who may touch what, and git becomes an internal implementation detail. (2) The graph is a set of TEMPORARY LOCAL repos, pushed upstream only once work is done and no conflicts exist. (3) Each session opens a TEMPORARY WORKTREE BRANCH holding an identical copy of the graph; the person works there, then reflow2's own merge reconciles the copy back and the temporary is deleted. (4) A WEBSOCKET pushing every change to every user, giving live simultaneous collaboration. WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE, and it matters for ranking them: the collision is in the export FILE, not in the graph, and reflow2 already answers file-level collision semantically — BL-80's three-way merge compares per node and per property against the common ancestor and mints each real conflict as a Question with a deterministic id, and `--merge`/`--merge-apply` run it without a server. So idea 3 is not new machinery; it is mostly a PROCEDURE over machinery that exists, and a git worktree already gives each person their own checkout with its own `.reflow2/graph` (the store lock is per-directory). The missing piece is small and specific: git supports per-path merge drivers — this repo already uses `merge=union` for COORD.md — so registering the design export with a driver that calls reflow2's own merge would make two people working different clusters merge automatically, and make a genuine overlap arrive as a Question instead of as conflict markers in a 500KB JSON file. Idea 2 is idea 3 with extra steps, since git branches are already local until pushed. Idea 1 would make reflow2 a version-control system, contradicts dec:repo-file-embedded and req:persistence, and would have to reinvent what it currently inherits for free. Idea 4 is the simultaneity road already held open by dec:central-host and BL-99, with the counter-argument recorded there: this tool's loop is deliberate and attributable rather than live.
properties.name: OPEN — how are two people's simultaneous edits kept apart: worktrees, temporary repos, or a live channel?
properties.rationale: Held as brainstorming on purpose. Anthony called it thinking out loud, and the first honest thing to do with four ideas is to write them down as four ideas rather than pick one and start building — which is precisely the practice dec:exploratory-staging is about. Two notes for whoever takes it up. The ranking above is a finding, not a decision: it says which ideas are cheap and which are large, and the cheap one is testable this week by two people on one design without a line of new Rust. And the doubt that started it should survive into whatever gets built — a claim on a cluster of nodes is not a claim on a repository, so any answer here has to say what happens to the CODE two people are writing beside the design, not only what happens to the graph.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED. Anthony, 2026-07-25: COORD.md was invented so he and his brother could coordinate; the claims layer shipped the same day; and reflow2 is developed by using reflow2 on itself, so the question is whether the markdown board should now be a graph read. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE, because it is less than it sounds: `claim_region` records a Contributor holding a seed node to a depth, `claim_report` computes the region and the overlaps, and both travel in the committed export exactly as COORD.md travels in git — so visibility is unchanged, and the gain is that the region is COMPUTED from the design (it follows the graph as the design moves) rather than being a hand-typed list of file paths that goes stale silently. WHAT WOULD BE LOST, and it is the part worth deciding rather than assuming: COORD.md is readable by a human with no reflow2 and no binary, it shows up as a diff in a pull request, and it holds the merge-conflict doctrine for the shared records — none of which a graph read does. The sane split, if this is taken: claims in the graph for WHO HAS WHAT, COORD.md retained for the conventions and the conflict doctrine, and the in-progress table deleted rather than maintained in two places, since two places for the same fact is the failure the backlog-in-the-graph move exists to end.
properties.name: OPEN — does reflow2's own claim board move from COORD.md into the graph?
properties.rationale: Raised as a dogfooding question, which is how most of this project's real findings have arrived — and it is a genuinely good test of the claims layer, because reflow2's own two-person collaboration is the only live multi-writer case that exists. Held proposed because a claim board is a coordination mechanism between two people, and switching it unilaterally would mean one of them silently changing where the other must look; that is Anthony's brother's call as much as his. The prerequisite is honest: nobody has used claim_region for real yet, so the first move is to run it on one real piece of work and see whether claim_report says something a person would have said.

properties.decision: ifc:core-api — the DesignGraph API cmp:graph provides and the MCP service consumes — is the sole operational path between the Design Store and the Agent Surface subsystems. Accepted as a SPOF, like dec:graph-spof-accepted and dec:service-spof-accepted.
properties.name: The DesignGraph API is an accepted single point of failure
properties.rationale: One store, one surface over it (req:agent-native, single-writer storage): the bridge between them is inherently single. Surfaced when BL-83a retired cmp:core and moved the API's provider to cmp:graph; the topology is honest, not a defect to engineer away.

properties.decision: DECIDED (b) THE SP-3b HANDSHAKE, on Anthony's word 2026-07-27. `ingest` goes on the MCP surface with the AGENT as the backend: reflow2 returns the extraction prompts and the agent returns the JSON. No LLM provider dependency is added, so the agent-native deferral stands. (a) an agent-driven skill walking the folder was rejected, not unconsidered: it is cheaper and consistent with every other reflow2 skill, but it moves the disciplines ingest.rs enforces IN CODE — never cascade-fail, no phantom edges, provenance on everything, time-aware resolution, and now the resolution bands and the structural subset pass — into prose an agent is asked to follow. An instruction is weaker than a type system, and docs/sharpening.md names that exact failure: shaping the model until the tool goes quiet. THE DECIDING CONSEQUENCE is what it does to the missing extraction passes: a pass written in Rust behind the handshake is reusable by every future ingest and testable without a model, while the same pass written into a skill is prose that cannot be regression-tested at all. Since Decision and Verification passes are the two-thirds of the requester's ask that reflow2 cannot currently see, the option that makes those passes worth writing is the option that delivers the feature.
properties.name: A folder of documents goes through the ingest handshake, not a skill
properties.rationale: Scoped 2026-07-26 by reading ingest.rs, graph.rs and the schema after Anthony asked whether reflow2 could take a colleague's years of markdown. The reading moved the work in BOTH directions. (1) BL-97 called cross-document identity the hard part; it is largely BUILT — fuzzy_match resolves each extracted node against every existing node of that type in the whole graph, so ingesting forty specs already converges, with the merges reported and prior states snapshotted rather than clobbered. What is missing there is COST, not capability: scan_nodes is a full type scan run once per extracted node, so a corpus is quadratic. (2) The gap nobody had named is COVERAGE OF THE ASK: ingest creates exactly eight node types, and Verification and Decision are not among them. The request was 'requirements, test results, designer intent' — reflow2 extracts the first and neither of the others, so a corpus run today would return a design with no test evidence and no rationale, from documents containing both, and nothing would say so. Full write-up in docs/scope-corpus-ingest.md, including the auto-merge-at-90 tension with dec:ask-not-repair at corpus scale, and the fifth instance of this project's recurring shape: the schema's per-type resolution thresholds are declared and read by nothing.

properties.decision: The design's authorship identity is a new first-class Contributor node type (kind: person / automated_agent / organization), kept separate from the existing Actor. Actor is who the designed system SERVES (boundary-facing domain content); Contributor is who authors and decides the design ITSELF. The first rung is the authorship seed: an AUTHORED_BY edge (any design node → Contributor, role author/reviewer/approver) — the structured "who" behind provenance's "how", replacing the free-text Requirement.source. AUTHORED_BY is deliberately NOT a traceability edge (absent from nodes.rs structural_rule), so authorship is metadata and never enlarges a blast radius. Later rungs, each needing the user on vocabulary: CLAIMS (BL-44 node/cluster claims, advisory-first), ACTS_FOR (agent-acts-for-person, git's author/committer split), alternative-authorship (BL-70), and signing the export content_hash with a Contributor key (BL-41 mechanical half). No "unauthored node" detector yet — it would N-alarm on every existing node.
properties.name: Design-authorship is a Contributor, distinct from an Actor; the seed is AUTHORED_BY
properties.rationale: User chose the identity keystone as the next most important work (2026-07-22), and decided both axes: a new type over overloading Actor, and authorship-first over jumping to claims. First-class node over a bare property because a claim expires and authorship belongs on axis-Z — a property is invisible to history. One identity mechanism because the backlog's own warning is that building it for claims alone would be "the recurring lesson in reverse": the same who-is-this is needed by BL-44 (claims), BL-70 (alternative authorship), BL-41 (the mechanical half of requirement-certainty, cultural today), and BL-12 sketch 2 (who may assert what). Contributor separate from Actor because they have different lifecycles — a UAF model keeps who-serves and who-makes apart. The git exploration (2026-07-22) independently ratified the shape: git's author-vs-committer split is exactly the deferred ACTS_FOR rung, and signing the record hash is BL-41's mechanical half. Additive schema change (28 node / 55 edge types); a new-binary graph is refused loudly by a pre-Contributor binary via the count-based provenance check (BL-19), so no schema_version bump.

properties.decision: A design-vs-design diff (compare_designs) exists as a core op exposed as both an MCP tool and a CLI flag. It compares two export documents, or the live graph against one document. Findings are directional — added / removed / changed relative to an explicitly named base — with property-level detail on changed nodes, grouped into two bands: design content vs the supporting/bookkeeping layer (ChangeEvents, DriftEvents, Fragments, Questions). It reports divergence between two as-designed records and never judges which side is right; the word 'drift' stays reserved for design-vs-reality.
properties.name: Design-vs-design comparison is directional, banded, and lives in the core
properties.rationale: User decided all four axes 2026-07-21 (BL-71 rung c vocabulary session). Directional because all three consumers have a real base — the committed record (the BL-71 clobber tripwire), the main branch (BL-70 branch-by-file comparison), the state a claim was made against (BL-12 merge) — while AoA can still read the report neutrally or run it both ways. Banded because the real 2026-07-21 divergence was 3 Decisions and 8 Requirements buried under ~20 bookkeeping nodes; a flat list hides exactly what matters. Core op (not a kit script) because deterministic design computation belongs in the tested core; CLI flag so CI and no-server contexts reach it, like --import/--export. It is the read side of the rung a+b upsert-layering, the sibling of the reconcile family — which compares design against reality, hence the separate word: divergence, not drift.

properties.decision: The Documentation subsystem, its docs component, the capability of explaining reflow2 to a newcomer, and the README/SETUP artifacts read as a disconnected community to `detect_defects`, and that reading is ACCEPTED rather than bridged. The cluster is correctly modelled: the project contains the subsystem, the subsystem contains the component, the component owns the capability, and the artifacts both REALIZE the capability and DOCUMENT the project, the installer and the service. Those DOCUMENTS edges are true and are kept on their own merit — the tool's own guidance is to record a file that way when something would be wrong if it drifted out of step with the design, which is exactly the property the user asserted when he said documentation is part of the deliverable. They simply do not attach the cluster, because the structural network is built from DEPENDENCY relations only (a direct DEPENDS_ON, or a CONSUMES/PROVIDES contract collapsed through its Interface), and documenting a thing is not depending on it. No further edge can fix this without being a lie: documentation genuinely does not participate in the operational dependency graph.
properties.name: Documentation is part of the product but has no operational coupling, so its island is accepted — and the detector should learn this
properties.rationale: Decided 2026-07-24, immediately after the user answered that documentation belongs to reflow2 rather than sitting outside it ("it'd be like if I designed a fighter jet using reflow2, but then didn't deliver any documentation on it to the user"). Three bridges were attempted before accepting: project containment, which is how every other subsystem attaches; then DOCUMENTS edges to the project, the installer and the service. The detector still fired, and reading structure.rs explains why — the design network admits a defined TRACEABILITY set (SATISFIES, ALLOCATED_TO, REALIZES, VERIFIES, GOVERNED_BY, PROVIDES/CONSUMES, DEPENDS_ON, INCLUDES) and DOCUMENTS is simply not in it, while CONTAINS is deliberately excluded. That selectivity is correct and should not be weakened to silence this. THE GENERAL PRINCIPLE, which is why this is worth recording rather than shrugging at: dec:operational-spof already established that only things which OPERATE can be single points of failure, because the suggested fix — add redundancy — is meaningless for intent. The identical argument applies one category over. Only things that operate can be meaningfully disconnected FROM the operational network; a documentation subsystem has no operational coupling by its nature, so flagging it is a false positive of the BL-84 family, and the fix belongs in the detector rather than in the design. RESOLVED 2026-07-25, and NOT by the fix this decision anticipated — recorded because a decision that goes on claiming to accept something that no longer happens is exactly the drift this project exists to catch. The island dissolved on its own when cap:session-memory turned out to belong to BOTH cmp:docs and cmp:temporal: the user's point that a session's context is itself documentation gave documentation a genuine, non-cosmetic tie to the rest of the design, through ALLOCATED_TO edges that are true rather than manufactured. So the detector was never wrong about the topology — the topology changed, because the design gained a real connection it had been missing. The PRINCIPLE above stands unaltered and still applies to any future documentation-only cluster; only the specific defect it dispositioned has gone. Worth keeping as evidence for the detector fix: an island can be legitimate AND later dissolve legitimately, so the exemption must not be written in a way that hides a genuine disconnection.

properties.decision: Standing rule for the edge vocabulary: two edge types must be orthogonal, because an LLM asked to choose between near-synonyms picks inconsistently (storyflow's lesson). The test for keeping any distinction is not 'is it true?' but 'does a computation — a detector, a report, a propagation rule — read the two sides differently?' If nothing reads it, the distinction is descriptive decoration that costs extraction consistency for no gain (the 'read side was blind' lesson turned on the vocabulary itself). Applied 2026-07-22: (1) RETIRE the VALIDATES edge — it was orthogonal-in-name-only with VERIFIES (both land Verification->Capability, the canonical V&V confusion) AND orphan (no core code ever referenced it). The verify-vs-validate distinction is real and worth keeping, so it moves to a Verification.kind property (verification | validation) — a property of the check, not a rival relationship, which removes the edge-choice ambiguity entirely — and it earns its keep via a new unvalidated_capability DETECT gap that reads it (a capability verified against spec but with no validation check confirming it meets intent). (2) FOLD ENABLES into CAUSES — same causal axis, differ only by degree (brings-about vs makes-possible), both wildcard-typed, and neither read by any computation; CAUSES's hint now covers the enabling case. (3) KEEP TRIGGERS — it is not a causal-degree variant: it carries a role property and drives the Flow/process-feedback model (flow_report, BL-37), so a computation reads it. Net: 55 -> 53 edge types; the 'does a computation read it?' test is the standing rule for any future edge.
properties.name: A vocabulary distinction earns its keep only if a computation reads it; retire VALIDATES + ENABLES edges
properties.rationale: User raised it from the storyflow lesson that edge types an agent chooses between must be completely orthogonal, and reasoned each case by cost/benefit: keeping a distinction buys nothing over collapsing unless a computation reads it, and sharpening extraction hints only lowers the error rate on a distinction that still has no reader — it cannot make a same-axis distinction orthogonal. VALIDATES was the clearest case: confusable AND orphan (the engine runs entirely on VERIFIES). Moving it to Verification.kind is strictly better than a rival edge because verify-vs-validate is an attribute of one check, not two relationships — as an edge it forces the confusable choice every time; as a kind there is always exactly one edge (VERIFIES). But a kind with no reader is the same orphan relocated, so it is kept only because the unvalidated_capability gap reads it — the mission-assurance question 'built to spec, but is it the right thing?', which the user's domain cares about. ENABLES vs CAUSES had no reader (0 core files each), so sharpening hints bought only cleaner extraction of a distinction nothing uses; collapsing removes the error class. TRIGGERS was rescued from the trio because it genuinely has a reader (its process role). The gap follows the BL-73 anti-flood lesson: one project-level rollup ('N verified capabilities have no validation check'), acknowledgeable once, not N per-capability alarms.

properties.decision: OPEN (proposed): the storage mechanism for planned epochs is undecided, and deciding it by drift would repeat the mistake BL-100 names. Three candidates are on the table, none chosen.
properties.name: Where does a planned epoch live — a git branch, the graph, or both?
properties.rationale: (a) EPOCH BRANCHES, Anthony's first framing: a git branch per planned epoch holding the expected export — full-document snapshots, diffable with the delta machinery, zero schema change; cost: the roadmap lives outside the graph, invisible to detectors, and n branches of a mutable file invite the lineage problems BL-107 closed. (b) IN-GRAPH FUTURE EPOCHS: Epoch nodes with future sequences, planned nodes pinned AT_EPOCH, the unused ANTICIPATES edge (confidence property) finally reached; roadmap visible to detect_gaps and propagate; cost: no single handable document, and axis-Z was built pointing backward. (c) HYBRID: roadmap in-graph, planned epochs exported to refs on demand; cost: two representations that can drift. AMENDED 2026-07-28, same day, after Anthony's second pass: git already does versions/tags/releases well (industry ships small increments fast — his brother's project, ~2 minors/week), which strengthens git as the SNAPSHOT STORE — but his bottom line reframes the choice: the graph must be the INDEX (see req:graph-indexes-snapshots), so the real shape is likely (c-refined): git stores snapshots under refs it is already good at, the graph owns the map from epoch_n/increment_n to ref plus the planned content, and a user never remembers a branch name. The rel:v0180 <-> tag v0.18.0 pattern is this exact division of labor, already shipping, pointed backward. Still OPEN: whether (b)'s in-graph planned content is required for detectors to reason about the roadmap, or whether the index alone suffices. THIRD AMENDMENT, same day: Anthony's satisfaction-schedule distillation shrinks what a planned epoch has to BE. If the roadmap's atom is 'requirement X expected/required satisfied at epoch_n' — a dated pin with a modality and a confidence — then the plan's content is a set of edges the graph holds natively (AT_EPOCH / ANTICIPATES with confidence), NOT a full expected-graph snapshot per epoch; the full snapshot becomes a DERIVED view (render the graph as of the pins that hold at epoch_n), which further strengthens (c-refined): the graph owns pins and index, git stores any rendered snapshot a human wants to hold in their hands, and nothing stores the same truth twice.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED as a vocabulary question, but MUCH SMALLER than it looked, and the skill that tests it is BUILT (2026-07-25, the brainstorm skill). REFRAMED by Anthony the same day, and the reframe was the useful part: what he and his brother were asking for is not a staging GATE, it is a KIND. "I think I now realize what my brother's idea was trying to say — it is like a brainstorming session where you can work through ideas without committing to anything yet. These would be more like 'ideas' not yet fleshed out and could be held in the graph as just that, 'brainstorming ideas'." That dissolves the contradiction this decision was opened over: the git study rejected the index because a gate between every edit and the graph is where intent goes to be forgotten, whereas a brainstorm is the opposite move — the idea DOES enter the graph, immediately, labelled as what it is. Nothing waits outside, so nothing is lost, and the design still never claims a half-formed thought as intent. THE FINDING THAT SHRANK THE QUESTION, from reading the detector while building the skill: the existing vocabulary ALREADY tells a musing from a choice, and a computation already reads the difference. `detect_gaps` raises `undecided_decision_point` only on a proposed Decision holding TWO OR MORE REGISTERED ALTERNATIVES — a fork with a real design export behind each branch (detect.rs: `alts.len() < 2 { continue }`). A proposed Decision whose options live in its prose therefore raises NO gap at all. So brainstormed ideas are silent by construction, and the nudge to choose arrives exactly when the ideas stop being ideas: register_alternative turns an option into a fork, and being asked to decide a fork is correct. Nobody has to remember which is which, and no label was needed to get it. WHAT A `brainstorm` KIND WOULD STILL BUY, and it is now a short list rather than the four-item one recorded yesterday: (a) delivery and certainty counts already exclude Decisions, so nothing is owed there; (b) gap silence is already delivered, per the finding above; (c) what remains is RETIREMENT — an idea nobody has touched in months could be surfaced as a candidate for tidying rather than sitting in the decision list forever, which is a real computation and the only one left standing; and (d) READABILITY — a person scanning 70-odd Decisions cannot tell at a glance which were choices and which were musings, which the skill currently answers with a sentence of prose inside the node rather than with a queryable property. PRIOR FRAMING, KEPT because it was true when written: the ask read as an opt-in "think first, commit later" mode; a session making no write calls IS rubber-ducking and the read tools are the ducking aids; and the narrow question was what happens at the END — which the skill now answers as a PROMOTION step, not a commit step.
properties.name: OPEN — do half-formed ideas get a place in the graph, distinct from things the design asserts?
properties.rationale: Raised by Anthony and his brother 2026-07-24, reframed by Anthony 2026-07-25, and the skill built the same day on his word ("go ahead with the brainstorm skill"). Built as a SKILL and not a schema change deliberately: it tests the practice at the cost of prose, and if the practice sticks the vocabulary question can be answered with evidence instead of taste — whereas a new node type or an enum value would have bought an upgrade doc and a foundation-migration checklist for a noun nobody had used yet. The evidence for the feature is this session itself: Anthony produced four isolation ideas he explicitly did not want to commit to, and the only home for them was a proposed Decision. That worked (dec:concurrent-work-isolation), which is why this is not urgent; it is also a slightly wrong fit, since a Decision node is meant for a choice someone is actually facing, and knowing exactly which part of the fit is wrong is what the finding above now pins down. Left PROPOSED because two of the four original arguments for a kind have dissolved and the remaining two (retirement candidates, at-a-glance readability) are real but small — and whether they are worth a schema change is Anthony's call, not a judgement to be made by the agent that just wrote the skill.

properties.decision: cmp:export and ifc:graph-export are the only route from a design to the kit converter (cmp:init) and to any other machine or reflow2 version, and they stay that way. Both single_point_of_failure warnings are accepted as intentional, not resolved by adding a second export path.
properties.name: The export document is an accepted single door, so its chain is an accepted SPOF
properties.rationale: dec:repo-file-embedded made the deterministic export the durable, diffable record, and req:survives-upgrade makes export-with-the-old-build / import-with-the-new THE migration mechanism — a single door is the feature, because a second export path would be a second source of truth for what the design is, and byte-identical determinism (req:persistence: a backup under git shows what actually changed) is only a meaningful promise about one format. The detector is right that severing this chain cuts cmp:init off from the design; that fragility is the price of one canonical portability format, knowingly paid. Accepted 2026-07-21 while dispositioning BL-69's corrected findings; sibling of dec:service-spof-accepted and dec:graph-spof-accepted.

properties.decision: Every export carries a content_hash — sha256 over the canonical sorted JSON of the design content only (graph_id, nodes, edges), excluding the stamp and chain fields, so the same design hashes identically whichever build wrote it. A prev_content_hash records file lineage: when an export overwrites an existing export file, the chain advances to the old file's content hash — but only when content actually changed, so two exports of an unchanged design stay byte-identical. The full hash is carried (not truncated like display checksums) because this is tamper evidence. compare_designs reports ancestry from the chain (other succeeds base / base succeeds other / siblings of a common parent / unknown); import reports an integrity mismatch loudly; the CI gate fails on a committed export that does not match its own hash. Documents predating the hash stay importable and comparable — absence is reported, never an error.
properties.name: The export proves itself: content hash + file-lineage chain, from AT proto's self-authenticating repos
properties.rationale: User directed 2026-07-21 after the AT Protocol comparison: atproto repos are self-authenticating (signed commits over a content-addressed root), and reflow2's export was already deterministic — the hash was well-defined and simply never computed. Content-only hashing (stamp excluded) was proven necessary the same day: the committed export and the live export had identical content but different writers (0.8.0 script vs 0.7.0-era session server), and they must fingerprint the same. The chain lives at the file-write seam because the committed export file IS the durable record whose lineage matters; the graph itself must not be mutated by a read-only export. Ancestry is what turns compare_designs from 'what diverged' into 'was the divergence made in ignorance of the base or in defiance of it' — BL-12 sketch idea 1's question, computable for the one-step case. Signing (identity) is deliberately deferred until a second writer is real; a hash chain without keys is already tamper-evident against accident and hand-editing, which is today's actual threat model.

properties.decision: The FNV-1a id hash (fnv1a) moves from cmp:detect (detect.rs) to cmp:nodes (nodes.rs), the vocabulary/identity leaf everything already sits above. This breaks the critical detect↔verify circular dependency: detect→verify is a genuine domain dependency (gap detection reads a capability's verification state, crate::verify::CapabilityVerification), but verify→detect existed ONLY because verify borrowed crate::detect::fnv1a to mint a deterministic id — not a domain dependency at all. Relocating the primitive removes that false edge (cycle broken, one-way detect→verify remains) and, as the same true consequence, removes five more fnv1a-only false couplings on cmp:detect (agent, artifact, drift, fielded, heal → detect all had no other detect reference); cmp:report keeps its real detect dependency (crate::detect::GapCandidate). Net self-model reconciliation: −6 DEPENDS_ON→cmp:detect, +1 cmp:agent→cmp:nodes (agent's new, real dependency on the primitive's home).
properties.name: The deterministic-id hash is a foundational primitive in nodes, not a detection concern — break the detect↔verify cycle by relocating it
properties.rationale: User directed fixing the critical cycle (2026-07-23). BREAK over ACCEPT because the cycle was not a genuine mutual dependency to live with — it was an artifact of a homeless utility: fnv1a began in detect.rs (where gap-id hashing first needed it) and eight modules reached through crate::detect::fnv1a, so the graph asserted a dependency on the detect DOMAIN that the code did not really have. Accepting it would embalm that lie; the honest move is to put the primitive where it belongs. RELOCATE-to-nodes over introduce-an-interface or invert-a-dependency because minting a derived node's id (gaps, heal issues, merge conflicts, prompts, drift/artifact keys) is an identity concern, and nodes is the vocabulary/identity module that is already a dependency leaf (depends on nothing), so the primitive gains no new coupling and creates no new cycle — the minimal, truthful home. The build script derives DEPENDS_ON from source (never prose), so a future rebuild reproduces exactly this shape; the committed self-model was reconciled by hand this session because it carries live-only nodes (req:nudge-covers-bypass, req:read-surfaces-debt) that block a full rebuild. Sibling in spirit to dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition (structure follows function/reality, not the file tree's accidents). The remaining structural defects are all accepted SPOFs and genuinely-disconnected intent clusters; this was the one critical one.

properties.decision: "The design as it stood at decision D" resolves by a three-step address: the Decision is pinned AT_EPOCH to a DesignEpoch, that epoch's existing `checksum` property carries the content_hash of the export cut there, and the document itself lives where it already lives — a git-committed reflow2.json. reflow2 supplies the coordinate; git supplies the bytes. No new node type, no mutable pointers, no reflow2-native DAG. Re-taking a road home is then the three-way merge already built (dec:merge-three-way), with the fork point as the base — which is precisely the merge-base reflow2 currently borrows from git, now derivable from its own epoch chain.
properties.name: A fork point is a coordinate (decision → epoch → export hash), not a stored copy or a native ref layer
properties.rationale: User decided 2026-07-24, choosing the coordinate over a native ref/branch layer. THE REJECTED ALTERNATIVE: branch names as graph nodes — mutable pointers to epochs, a real DAG, so reflow2 finds its own merge-base without git. Rejected on two grounds. (1) It duplicates machinery git already provides, and dec:repo-file-embedded already put the design in the repo as a file precisely so the repo's tooling carries the file-shaped concerns; dec:merge-three-way already chose explicit inputs over git's DAG for the same reason. (2) A mutable pointer is a foreign object in this graph: the whole doctrine of axis Z is that history is never overwritten (req:intent-preserved, req:roads-not-taken), and a ref that moves is by construction a thing whose past value is lost unless separately recorded — reintroducing the erosion the epoch chain exists to prevent. The coordinate has the further virtue of costing nothing: DesignEpoch.checksum already existed in the schema, described as "a hash over the anchored spec set at this epoch", which is exactly this use. Honest limit: only exports from v0.9.0 on carry an embedded content_hash (dec:export-hash-chain shipped then), so epochs before it are addressed by git tag alone and claim no checksum rather than inventing one.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-07-25: "what if reflow2 was paired with github's mcp and two worked in tandem?" THE ARCHITECTURAL POINT FIRST, because it decides how expensive any of this is: MCP composes AT THE AGENT, not in the code. An agent can hold both servers at once, so reflow2 would never call GitHub and would never learn what a pull request is — the integration would live entirely in a SKILL that knows both surfaces exist. Zero coupling, no dependency, nothing in the core. Skills are now served from the binary, so such a skill costs a consumer project nothing. SIX PAIRINGS, strongest first. (1) THE PUBLISHING CASE — dec:nested-graphs says a design is its own graph per ownership boundary and designs link by mirroring a published surface, and the open question underneath dec:central-host was always "how does the other team REACH my surface without cloning my repo". GitHub is already that distribution network: an agent with github-mcp fetches another repo's committed export, and mirror_surface imports its published boundary with the coordinate. That is federation with no server, no hosting and no account beyond the one they already have — it may answer the strongest argument for hosting. (2) NOTIFICATION reflow2 structurally lacks — reflow2 can only nudge an agent that is already running, which is exactly req:nudge-path-proven's weakness; an unacknowledged gap posted as a GitHub issue reaches a PERSON who is not at a terminal, and closing that issue with an answer writes back through answer_question. (3) THE GATE EXPLAINS ITSELF IN REVIEW — today the coherence gate fails a build; with github-mcp the same finding becomes a review comment naming the thread ("this moves art:X, which realizes cap:Y, which satisfies req:Z — and req:Z has no verification"), landing where humans actually decide. (4) TRACEABILITY IN THE PR BODY — the golden thread from requirement to artifact, written where a reviewer sees WHY and not only what. (5) CLAIMS AGAINST REAL DATA — claim_report overlaps computed against open PRs' changed files rather than announcements, and dec:advisory-concurrency's "first-on-disk, both provable" has an exact GitHub expression in which PR opened first. (6) RELEASE NOTES DERIVED from the graph — delivered requirements and the decisions in that epoch, cut and attached by github-mcp. THE OBJECTIONS, recorded beside the ideas. Context cost is real: reflow2 serves 106 tools and github-mcp is comparably large, so an agent holding both pays in tool-selection noise — both have an answer (find_tools, and GitHub's toolsets/dynamic discovery, noted in docs/github-mcp-nuggets.md) and neither answer is free. And the load-bearing one: reflow2's proposition is that it works with no service and no account. Any pairing must be ADDITIVE AND NEVER REQUIRED, or reflow2 excludes GitLab, self-hosted, air-gapped and classified environments — which is the population this tool was built for.
properties.name: OPEN — does reflow2 run in tandem with GitHub's MCP server, and where would the pairing pay?
properties.rationale: Raised as brainstorming while looking at how two people collaborate over plain git, so nothing here is scheduled and nothing is promoted. Kept as ONE decision rather than six because the pairings are a menu under a single question — whether reflow2 reaches for a second MCP surface at all — and answering that decides the shape of every item. Worth recording rather than leaving in conversation because two of the six touch decisions already on the record: (1) bears directly on dec:central-host, where the publishing case is named as the strongest argument for hosting a server, and GitHub-as-distribution would weaken that argument without any hosting at all; (2) bears on req:nudge-path-proven, which is accepted work about a notification path reflow2 cannot currently prove reaches anybody. The architectural observation is the part most likely to be forgotten and re-derived: MCP integration happens in the agent's context, not in either server's code, so the whole idea is skill-shaped and reversible — which is also why it can be tried cheaply on one pairing before deciding anything.

properties.decision: cmp:graph is the single store handle everything else hangs off, and it stays that way. The single_point_of_failure warning on it is accepted as intentional, not resolved by adding redundancy.
properties.name: The graph handle is an accepted single point of failure
properties.rationale: The architecture is explicit (AGENTS.md): DesignGraph is 'the single handle everything else hangs off' — one schema-validated CRUD surface so every coherence-loop module speaks to one store one way. Removing it strands schema, search and vocabulary (each with its file) plus the export chain, which is the BL-69 detector telling the truth about the spine. Redundancy is incoherent here twice over: these are modules compiled into one binary (they cannot fail independently of cmp:graph at run time — the same reasoning as the F6 library filter, which cannot see cmp:graph only because it provides no Interface node), and a second graph handle would mean two write paths to one store, exactly the incoherence the single handle exists to prevent. Accepted 2026-07-21 while dispositioning BL-69's corrected findings; sibling of dec:service-spof-accepted.

properties.decision: A design's identity is a UUID minted at genesis and stored in the graph; the friendly name is a label on top of it. A seat's identity is the harness session id it was already given. Rejected: deriving from the project name or path (two designs can share both, and the id must survive being copied), and a registry that hands out ids (that is the coordination this avoids, and there is no service to host it).
properties.name: Names are assigned with zero coordination, never derived from shared state
properties.rationale: Neither identifier is negotiated with anybody, so neither can race — unique by construction at one seat or fifteen. The fleet reached this by DELETING a whole mint-race guard: the race was an artifact of deriving the handle by reading a shared roster, so removing the derivation removed the race rather than patching it. reflow2 has the derived-identity bug twice today — every in-memory graph answered DEFAULT_GRAPH_ID until mirroring needed open_in_memory_as, and claims record a label rather than an owner.

properties.decision: The install registers reflow2 with the agent at USER scope — the MCP server, the ten slash commands, the coherence-loop hooks and a `reflow2` command on PATH — so every project on the machine has it with no per-project setup. `reflow2_init.py` survives, but its job narrows: it writes the pointer file and project-scope config for a repo OTHER PEOPLE work on, so their agent is told reflow2 governs this code. Solo work needs none of it. Anthony's call, 2026-07-28, choosing "machine-wide, repo init optional" over "machine-wide only" and over "keep per-project, just make it one word".
properties.name: reflow2 installs once per machine; the in-repo half is optional and only for repos you share
properties.rationale:
WHY NOT "MACHINE-WIDE ONLY", which is simpler: a teammate cloning the repo would get no signal that reflow2 governs it unless they had already installed reflow2 themselves and thought to look. That is the invisibility `req:kit-reaches-the-agent` was raised for, and retiring the per-project installer would rebuild it deliberately.

WHY NOT "JUST MAKE IT ONE WORD" (`reflow2 init .` instead of a python path): it fixes the typing and none of the arithmetic. Still one step per project, still a re-run after every upgrade, and still the case that a user who forgets it experiences reflow2 as absent.

WHAT MADE MACHINE-WIDE SAFE TO CHOOSE AT ALL, and without it the answer would have been different: the server is registered with `--only-if-present`, so a directory that never opted into a design gets the LATENT surface and nothing is created in it. Without that flag, a user-scope registration would drop a RocksDB store into every folder a session is ever opened in — and litter in someone's repo is a worse first impression than the setup step it removed. The loop-nudge hook is gated the same way and for the same reason: registered globally, silent wherever `.reflow2/` does not exist.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE: `dec:skills-served` and `req:thin-install` stand exactly as they were. The skills and working instructions are still served, still never copied, and upgrading reflow2 still produces no diff in a consumer repo. This decision is about WHERE the pointers are installed, not about what is served — and it makes the thin install thinner, since the common case now installs nothing into a project at all.

properties.decision: PROPOSED as a proof of concept, Anthony 2026-07-27, captured while fresh rather than worked: build a reflow2 design graph inside storyflow (adopt is under way, not finished) and another inside dynograph-foundation, then have an agent LINK them through their published surfaces and identify where the interfaces are incompatible. THE CASE IS WELL CHOSEN AND NOT A TOY: reflow2 and storyflow BOTH depend on dynograph-foundation, so it is a real three-way seam between three real repositories with a real answer, and both consumers were built by the same author at different times against a foundation that moved — which is precisely how interface drift happens in the wild. Each project's graph would then PUBLISH ITS OWN INTERFACE SPEC, which is what any consumer needs and what makes the seam checkable. What this would actually prove, and why it is worth doing rather than arguing: whether dec:nested-graphs (a graph per ownership boundary) and cap:mirror-surface hold up on three designs nobody built to be composed. WHAT IT DEPENDS ON: req:interface-spec-complete first — reflow2 structures roughly one and a half of the six characteristics an interface spec needs and puts the rest in one free-text string, so today two graphs can be linked and still not be comparable. Then req:seam-incompatibility, which is the finding the PoC is meant to produce.
properties.name: OPEN — prove composition on reflow2 + storyflow + dynograph-foundation
properties.rationale: Anthony's own framing, and it lands on intent reflow2 already holds: req:design-composes (accepted, blocked on dec:nested-graphs at the time), dec:nested-graphs (DECIDED — a design is its own graph when separately owned, released or shared, which is exactly three sibling repos), cap:mirror-surface and cap:publish-surface (both built). So the LINKING half exists and the COMPARING half does not. Recorded as a decision point rather than a plan because the sequencing is a real choice: structure the interface spec first and then run the PoC, or run the PoC against today's thin spec to find out what it cannot say. Also worth noting the PoC has a second payoff independent of the result — it is the first time reflow2 would be pointed at a design it did not author, twice, which is the adopt path Anthony says his real work almost always starts from.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-07-25, from work he has done: State Funerals for US Presidents (he worked President Bush's) — hundreds to thousands of people planning simultaneously, an echeloned plan (NORTHCOM OPLAN → JTF-NCR → each service → each unit), and events arriving during the run that the plan must react to in minutes. His words: "using a common github repo may no longer work". THE DECOMPOSITION THAT MAKES IT TRACTABLE IS ALREADY DECIDED: dec:nested-graphs (c) says a design is its own graph per ownership boundary, so a thousand planners are not a thousand writers on one store — they are ~100-200 graphs of 5-20 writers each, linked by mirrored published surfaces. Echelons own their plans; that is both the software answer and how the organisation actually works. FOUR ROADS for the tier itself. (a) NOTHING NEW — federation plus git, accepting minutes of latency; cheapest, and it fails only the react-in-near-real-time half. (b) ONE PROCESS PER GRAPH over streamable HTTP (rmcp has the transport, reflow2 serves stdio only), writes going to the store and the export DERIVED as the archival record; at federation scale the process-per-project cut already named in dec:central-host is also the natural sharding — one process per ownership boundary is one staff. (c) ONE SHARED MULTI-WRITER STORE, which means replacing single-writer RocksDB and owning consensus; most work, least alignment with a design that already shards by authority. (d) EVENT-SOURCED LOG plus materialised views — attractive because a plan IS a change history, expensive because every detector currently reads a materialised graph. WHAT BREAKS TODAY, in order: single-writer per graph (the six-seat outage of 2026-07-25 was this at tiny scale), the whole-document write path (769 KB for 606 nodes; a funeral federation is 10^5-10^6 nodes changing continuously), git-round-trip latency, nothing that pushes, no identity or authorization, and req:stale-seat-knows going from one bad afternoon to a systemic property.
properties.name: OPEN — does reflow2 grow a live tier for hundreds of simultaneous planners, alongside the repo file?
properties.rationale: Held as brainstorming because it is explicitly distant-future ("probably distant future") and because it challenges the PREMISE of two decisions rather than their reasoning — which is the honest thing to record, not to act on. dec:multi-writer-architecture chose repo-file-plus-merge on a rationale resting on concurrency being hypothetical; dec:central-host's rationale says outright that this tool "does not need" simultaneity "and may be harmed by it". A thousand people replanning a state funeral under events is the named counter-case both were missing, and per dec:reopen-supersedes the move is a new decision point, never flipping those back. NOTE THE PART THAT NEEDS NO DECISION: the ownership boundary federation already draws is the natural AUTHORIZATION boundary — you write your echelon's graph and read your superior's published surface — so authz needs enforcement, not a new concept, and Interface.designation internal|published is already the read primitive.
