Also settled by inspection: ordering without a shared git history needs no global clock, because the same federation shape gives a total order WITHIN each boundary (the store, proved by the content-hash chain) and dated coordinates ACROSS boundaries (a mirror already carries whose design, which version, when) — exactly how echelons coordinate. Full reasoning in docs/planning-at-scale.md.

properties.decision: loop_status reports what the coherence loop is owed — anchored gaps never surfaced, questions waiting or answered-but-unwritten, structural defects, capabilities claiming realized/verified with no passing check, drift awaiting disposition, claims never examined — computed entirely from current graph state. reflow2 does not track when tools were run: phase nudges are excluded (guidance, not debt), and the write tools carry static loop_hint pointers at the next loop step in their own results.
properties.name: Loop debt is computed from graph state, never from run history
properties.rationale: From the StoryFlow fleet trial (BL-74): under operational load the agent kept bookkeeping via raw tools while the loop skills silently stopped — 'a design-discipline tool that depends on being remembered will lose to operational urgency every time; fire on a trigger, not on virtue.' Run-history ('no detect_gaps since Tuesday') is not honestly computable here: the core takes no clock, and looking-is-not-writing is doctrine — recording reads so observation could be tracked would make looking mutate the record. Outstanding debt is the state-based equivalent and the actionable truth regardless of who ran what when. The hint rides the tool result the agent already reads (zero extra round-trip to see it), and loop_status is the cheap computation a client hook can fire on its own events — rung a of the BL-74 ladder builds on exactly this call. Decided 2026-07-21.

properties.decision: The three-way merge (cap:merge-designs, dec:merge-three-way) resolves per node, per property, and per edge against the base by this case table. NODES/PROPERTIES: only one side changed a property -> take it; both changed it differently -> conflict. add/add (same id, no base) -> treated as modify/modify against an empty base: matching properties merge, each differing property is a conflict. delete/delete -> node gone, no conflict. delete/modify (one side removes the node, the other changes it) -> RETAIN-AND-ASK: the proposal keeps the modified node and raises a conflict asking the human to confirm the deletion or keep it, leaning toward keeping — deletion is the destructive side and must be re-justified, never the silent default (req:intent-preserved, retire-vs-delete). Symmetric in both directions. EDGES: first-class design content and get the identical three-way rule — one-sided add or remove -> take it; the same edge changed differently on both sides, or one side removes while the other changes it -> conflict; never silently drop an edge one side deliberately cut (req:no-silent-fallback). CONFLICT REPRESENTATION: a both-sides conflict is a Question node with source 'merge_conflict', a deterministic id (FNV over base + node/edge id + property, the existing gap-id normalization), carrying the base/ours/theirs values; it reuses the existing answer_question / open_questions machinery and writes nothing until dispositioned, and its normalized id is the key a later rerere rung (BL-80 #5) replays a recorded resolution against. No new node type — the schema stays 28.
properties.name: The merge conflict case table: retain-and-ask on delete, edges symmetric with nodes, conflicts are Questions
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22, each the doctrine-aligned option, closing the sub-decisions dec:merge-three-way explicitly deferred. Retain-and-ask over a neutral conflict because losing a node is not symmetric with keeping it: req:intent-preserved and the retire-vs-delete distinction make a delete the move that must be justified, so the proposal keeps the node and asks rather than treating erasure as an equal default. Edges symmetric with nodes because they carry the golden thread — a lighter union-and-keep-wins rule would override a deliberate one-sided edge removal without asking, which is exactly the silent drop req:no-silent-fallback forbids; compare_designs already bands edge divergence, so the input is there. Reuse Question over a dedicated MergeConflict type for the recurring schema-minimalism reason (the vocabulary was already sufficient — same lesson as dec:certainty-derived and dec:component-verified-computed): the answer/open-questions machinery, the deterministic FNV gap-id normalization, and the human-decides routing all already exist, and reusing them makes the conflict rerere-ready for free (BL-80 #5) while keeping the schema at 28 node types. With this, the merge is fully specified — nothing left but the build and its verification.

properties.decision: reflow2 records how a human resolved a merge conflict and offers it back when the same conflict recurs (git's rerere), on three axes the user decided. (1) STORAGE — in the graph, as an answered Question (source=merge_resolution) whose id IS the conflict's content fingerprint: reuses the answer_question/open_questions machinery, travels with the design in the export, no schema change (stays 28 node types) — exactly what dec:merge-conflict-semantics anticipated ('reuse Question; its normalized id is the key a later rerere rung replays against'). (2) BEHAVIOR — advisory: a recorded resolution is surfaced as a suggestion on the matching conflict, and the human still confirms (dec:report-dont-judge, dec:three-party-checks). apply_merge applies only what it is given; an opt-in use_recorded lets the human bulk-accept every recorded suggestion in one move (the confirmation is passing the flag), and apply refuses if any conflict still has neither an explicit nor a recorded decision. (3) KEY — content only: the fingerprint is over (property, base value, ours value, theirs value), independent of which node, so ONE resolution replays across ALL nodes with the identical conflict — this is git's model and what delivers the motivating BL-73 win (20 near-identical conflicts, 21 near-identical hand-resolutions → resolve the shape once). apply_merge records every applied property/edge-property resolution keyed by content, so the memory grows as you work.
properties.name: rerere: record a conflict resolution content-keyed in the graph, replay it advisory-only
properties.rationale: User decided all three axes 2026-07-22, each the doctrine-aligned option. Content-only keying because it is the whole point: the BL-73 field pain was N near-identical conflicts across different nodes, and a per-node key would give near-zero reuse and miss exactly that case; content-only is git's proven model, and pairing it with advisory behavior keeps over-reach visible (the human sees each application). Advisory over auto-apply because the three-party doctrine puts the decision with the human — but the recorded suggestion plus a bulk-accept toggle kills the repetitive grind without silently resolving on the human's behalf. Reuse-Question over a new node type or a side cache is the recurring no-schema-change lesson AND keeps the memory inside the design that travels in the export (a side rr-cache would be a second source of truth that a teammate importing the design would not receive). Scoped in v1 to property and edge-property conflicts (a clear base/ours/theirs value triple, and the N-near-identical shape); node-type and delete/modify keys are deferred (no clean value triple), as is aging/pruning the memory. Extends cap:merge-designs; the conflict ids the merge already mints were built for exactly this (dec:merge-conflict-semantics).

properties.decision: When HEAL merges DUPLICATES-asserted nodes, the survivor is picked by provenance rank (authored > planned > imported > reconciled > inferred > healed); node id breaks ties. Pre-provenance graphs are unchanged.
properties.name: Merge survivor is chosen by provenance, id breaks ties
properties.rationale: User decided option 2 for BL-29 (2026-07-20): provenance is the closest thing the graph has to 'who asserted this and how deliberately'. Refinement from the 2026-07-20 self-adopt live session: a node with UNSET provenance defaults to authored, which made two genesis stubs tie against authored+verified survivors and nearly win on alphabetical id — set provenance explicitly on both sides before proposing a merge, and consider ranking unset below authored in a future revision.

properties.decision: The design merge is a three-way typed merge exposed as a core op (MCP tool + CLI flag), the write-side sibling of compare_designs. (1) Inputs are three explicit export documents — a common ancestor (base), ours, theirs; git supplies the base (git merge-base + the committed reflow2.json at that commit), so reflow2 does not build its own commit DAG for this rung. The multi-parent/ref layer that would let reflow2 find its own merge-base is deferred to BL-70/#3. (2) The algorithm is git's trivial-merge case table run per node and per property against the base over typed values, not lines: only one side changed a property -> take it; both sides changed it differently -> a structured conflict. (3) It produces a merge proposal — auto-resolved one-sided changes plus a list of both-sides conflicts rendered as Questions ('node X.prop Y: base=A, ours=B, theirs=C — which?') — and writes NOTHING to the graph. The human dispositions the conflict Questions, then an explicit apply commits the merge. Compare reports and never writes; merge does the same until the human has looked.
properties.name: The three-way merge takes explicit inputs over git's DAG, and reports a proposal it never auto-applies
properties.rationale: User decided both axes 2026-07-22, both the recommended option. Explicit-inputs-over-git because the exports are already git-committed (dec:repo-file-embedded) and git already tracks the merge-base — building a second DAG inside reflow2 would reimplement what git provides and contradicts 'export/import is the right-sized git bundle analogue' (BL-80's explicit do-NOT-import list). It keeps rung #1 shippable now and defers the ref/branch layer to where it belongs (BL-70). compare_designs already computes the typed per-property diff this consumes, so the input side is built. Report-a-proposal-never-auto-apply because a both-sides conflict IS a Question and the graph must not silently pick a side (dec:report-dont-judge, req:human-decides, req:no-silent-fallback); mirroring compare's read-only contract keeps the sibling honest, and the explicit apply is the disposition gate (dec:two-sided-accept's spirit — no silent write) without a staging area (BL-80 explicitly rejects the index). Typed per-node/per-property conflicts are strictly better than git's line markers — the key 'graph is not files' caveat. This specifies BL-12's merge problem: rung #1 (this algorithm over three documents) + #2 (the retained ancestor, here git's) = the L core of BL-12. Deferred to their own decisions: delete/modify and add/add conflict semantics (retire-vs-delete makes a delete meaningful, so delete/modify must go to the human, never auto-resolve), edge-merge banding, and the exact shape of the conflict Question.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED, RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING. Anthony, 2026-07-25, supplied the DoD MOSA Implementation Guidebook (OUSD(R&E) Systems Engineering and Architecture, February 2025, Distribution A) and was explicit about the frame: "just taking principles, concepts and ideas from this. not looking to implement mosa exactly over this document." So this records what the guidebook's concepts illuminate about reflow2, not a plan to become a MOSA tool. THE DEFINITION IT GIVES: "an acquisition and design approach consisting of a technical and business architecture that supports using system interfaces compliant with widely supported and consensus-based standards... A MOSA system structure allows for severable components to be incrementally added, removed, or replaced throughout the life cycle" (10 U.S.C. 4401, mandated for all DoD acquisition programs to the maximum extent practicable). ITS FIVE-STEP FRAMEWORK is a process, not a document: Plan, Modularize, Identify Interfaces, Define Interfaces, Standardize Interfaces — and reflow2 can already model a process rather than only a product (cap:model-process, Flow nodes), so the framework is expressible as a Flow whose steps the graph can be checked against. THE FINDING THAT MATTERS, from Table D-1 "MOSA Conformance Criteria and Verification Methods": most of what MOSA asks a program to demonstrate, reflow2 already computes for other reasons. Their MODULARITY criterion — "encapsulated, cohesive, loosely coupled, and organized into functional categories" — is the Leiden modularity score, community detection and the god-component detector that graph_report already prints. Their MOSA OBJECTIVES criterion — "demonstrate severable modular components" — is propagate_change: if the blast radius of a change inside a module stops at that module's interfaces the module is severable, and if it leaks past them the module is not modular whatever the architecture diagram says. That is severability as a COMPUTED property rather than an assertion, which is the same move dec:certainty-derived made for requirement status and cap:derived-completion made for delivery. Their MOSA MODULES criterion — "implement minimal functions, are functionally independent, encapsulated, and traceable to requirements" — is the god-component detector plus the golden thread. Their LIFE CYCLE CHARACTERISTICS criterion — severable, replaceable, interoperable, allowing competition — is the severability computation plus the alternatives layer, where interchangeable suppliers behind one interface are exactly an analysis of alternatives. WHAT IS GENUINELY MISSING, and it is one vocabulary item and one check. (1) NOTHING MARKS AN INTERFACE AS KEY. MOSA's whole discipline turns on designating major/modular system interfaces and then holding them stable and open; reflow2 has Interface nodes, provides/consumes and SPECIFIES, but no way to say "this one is the published boundary and that one is internal plumbing". BL-45 found the identical hole from the opposite direction — external dependencies between reflow2 projects — and recorded it as "nothing marks an Interface external-facing". Two independent routes to one missing property is the strongest evidence this design has for a vocabulary addition. (2) NOTHING CHECKS STANDARDS COMPLIANCE, and the vocabulary for it is present and unused: DesignRule is defined as a chosen standard or convention with an `enforced` flag, and there are zero DesignRules in any graph — the same schema-present-practice-absent shape as the temporal axis and the KPP vocabulary before them. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded beside the idea rather than used to bury it: MOSA is domain vocabulary for defence acquisition, and req:design-anything says the vocabulary stays neutral. A MOSA conformance report is therefore a VIEW — a projection over computations that already exist, in the acquisition community's words — and not a set of new node types. Building it as a view keeps the core neutral (dec:views-are-projections) and any renderer fill-in remains a defect. If it were ever built as schema, reflow2 would have taken on one domain's language as its own, which is the thing it has refused since the beginning.
properties.name: OPEN — should reflow2 report MOSA conformance, given it already computes most of the criteria?
properties.rationale: Recorded 2026-07-25 as brainstorming from the DoD MOSA Implementation Guidebook Anthony supplied, on his framing: principles and concepts, not an implementation of MOSA. PROMOTED THE SAME DAY on his word ("let's promote both") into the two things the guidebook actually exposed as missing, both now accepted: req:key-interfaces (the design says which interfaces are the published boundaries, and computations read the distinction) and req:modularity-computed (severability and cohesion are computed from the graph, not asserted by the diagram). Both are GOVERNED_BY this decision. WHAT STAYS OPEN is the question this decision was opened on, and it is narrower now: whether reflow2 ships a MOSA-BRANDED report. The requirements are domain-neutral by construction — published boundary, severable part — so they can be built without answering it, and the acquisition community's words for the same criteria belong in a view over the computation rather than in the schema (dec:views-are-projections, req:design-anything). Deciding otherwise would adopt one domain's language as reflow2's own, which is the thing it has refused since the beginning. SEQUENCING, and it is not arbitrary: req:key-interfaces comes first because req:modularity-computed depends on it — severability is only checkable once the design knows where a boundary is. req:design-composes also links through published boundaries, so the same property serves the federation thread; that is the second independent route to it, after BL-45 found the identical hole from the system-of-systems side on 2026-07-20.

properties.alternatives: [{"option":"repo file, merge on pull","outcome":"chosen","note":"contradicts nothing; reuses the built merge machinery; needs BL-44 claims"},{"option":"hosted service","outcome":"rejected","note":"contradicts req:persistence and req:invocation (both accepted); supersedes dec:repo-file-embedded; design leaves the user's machine; permanent operational burden"},{"option":"hybrid: hosted coordination, local designs","outcome":"rejected","note":"keeps req:persistence but strains req:invocation with a second surface; the claims layer approximates the benefit without a server"}]
properties.decision: DECIDED 2026-07-25: the design STAYS a graph-in-a-repo-file, and many writers are handled by merging on pull. No hosted service, no shared writable store. Each person's design lives at ./.reflow2/graph in their own checkout, git moves it, and genuinely overlapping work is resolved by the three-way merge that already exists — typed per-node and per-property against the common ancestor, with each conflict minted as a Question carrying a deterministic id, and recorded resolutions replayable across near-identical conflicts (rerere). THIS CONFIRMS dec:repo-file-embedded RATHER THAN SUPERSEDING IT. That is the outcome worth noting: this was the first field-sourced re-opening of a settled decision, triggered because dec:repo-file-embedded's own rationale said the concurrency argument was 'hypothetical while there is one writer' and fifteen developers made it concrete. The precondition genuinely changed, the decision was genuinely re-opened, and the original answer survived contact with the new evidence. A re-opening that ends where it started is not wasted — it converts an assumption into a tested position. WHAT WAS REJECTED AND WHY. A HOSTED SERVICE: rejected on cost against confirmed intent, not on taste. It contradicts req:persistence ('the graph lives at ./.reflow2/graph inside the consumer project, so the design travels with the repo') and req:invocation ('the reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio, installed into a consumer project'), both accepted, so choosing it would have required retiring or revising confirmed intent rather than merely adding machinery. It also puts the design on a machine the user does not control, carries permanent operational burden, and breaks the session-transcript identity for everyone but the local user (a local path resolves for one person and silently misses for the rest). A HYBRID — hosted claims and presence over local designs: rejected as the weaker version of the same trade. It keeps req:persistence but strains req:invocation with a second surface to run, and buys live visibility that the claims layer can approximate without a server. WHAT THIS COMMITS TO BUILDING: the scoping primitive (BL-44 cluster claims) so two people do not collide in the first place, and merge-on-pull ergonomics. The honest weakness accepted with this choice: no live view of what others hold, so overlap surfaces at merge time rather than before it — which is exactly the trade git itself makes, and the one this project's users already understand.
properties.name: Many writers keep the repo file and merge on pull — no hosted service
properties.rationale: Raised by the user and his brother, 2026-07-24, from a concrete scenario rather than speculation. This is the first field-sourced trigger to re-open a settled decision, and it is worth recording WHY it counts as one: dec:repo-file-embedded's own rationale reads "the service's strongest argument (concurrency) is hypothetical while there is one writer." Fifteen developers is that hypothesis arriving, so the decision is not being second-guessed — its stated precondition has changed. That is exactly the signal cap:revise-trigger is being built to surface automatically; here it arrived by conversation instead, which is itself evidence the trigger is worth building. Held proposed deliberately: the architecture question is upstream of every feature beneath it (req:concurrent-planning among them), and starting to build under an unmade decision is how a design acquires an architecture nobody chose. The counter-argument that belongs in the weighing, so it is not lost: reflow2's loop is built around asking a human and recording an attributable answer — deliberate, sequential, credited — and simultaneous editing may be the wrong shape for that product even where it is technically reachable. What the raised scenario actually asks for is non-colliding parallel work plus good merges, which may be reachable without a service at all.

properties.decision: DECIDED 2026-07-25 by Anthony: option (c), A GRAPH PER OWNERSHIP BOUNDARY WITH LEVELS INSIDE EACH. A design is its own graph when something at that level is separately OWNED, separately RELEASED, or separately SHARED — and a subtree of one graph otherwise. The hierarchy does not decide; authority does. That is the shape federated systems engineering actually uses, and it makes the split rule non-arbitrary: you can always answer "why is this its own design?" with a name, a release train, or a recipient. WHAT FOLLOWS, and each is an obligation rather than a detail. (1) THE COORDINATE. Edges cannot cross stores because the schema validates both endpoints, so a link between designs is not an edge: the other side's published surface is MIRRORED into your graph as local nodes, and the mirror carries the coordinate — which design it came from, at what content hash, when. Your own components then PROVIDE and CONSUME the mirrored Interface with ordinary local edges, so the golden thread works unchanged and foreignness is a property of the NODE rather than of the link. Same reasoning as dec:fork-point-address: a coordinate resolved against a document, never a live ref layer. (2) ROLL-UP. A parent's view of a composed child must derive from the child's own evidence or a requirement satisfied inside the child fires unsatisfied in the parent forever — cap:derived-completion's computation one level up. (3) FRESHNESS. A mirror is a dated claim about a VERSION, so a newer surface with a different hash makes it stale and that must be detectable, never assumed current (the cap:freshness and confirmation-ledger shape). (4) THE SEAM. Two teams changing the boundary itself still collide, in the one place the merge machinery does not reach; the published-surface document is what they are actually negotiating over. THE ROADS NOT TAKEN, kept because req:roads-not-taken says they are part of the record. (a) ONE GRAPH, ZOOM BY LEVEL was not rejected — it was BUILT FIRST and remains correct for everything inside one ownership boundary; cap:scoped-analysis delivers it, and (c) is a superset rather than a replacement. What (a) alone could not do is give two owners separate write locks, separate release trains, or a way to share one part without sharing everything. (b) A GRAPH PER SYSTEM was rejected as a RULE, not as a possibility: a system that is separately owned still gets its own graph under (c), but depth alone stops being sufficient reason, because every seam costs a coordinate, a roll-up and a freshness check, and a three-level tower of graphs inside one team buys none of what those cost. THE TENSION THIS RESOLVES, and it should be resolved out loud: docs/org-scale-vision.md records the destination as "one graph the whole company plans in". Under (c) that is no longer the destination — an enterprise is many designs federated at ownership boundaries, and the CEO's objectives are one design that others mirror rather than one graph everyone writes into. That document now describes a road not taken and should say so.
properties.name: DECIDED — a graph per ownership boundary, levels inside each
properties.rationale: Raised 2026-07-25 as brainstorming, because Anthony said plainly he was not convinced by the collaboration design and an unconvinced author is a finding rather than a disagreement to be argued down. Promoted to intent the same day, and COLLAPSED the same day on his word ("let's do (c) option"). THE SEQUENCE IS THE ARGUMENT for why this was worth holding open for a few hours rather than deciding immediately: option (a)'s scope filter was built FIRST precisely because it forecloses nothing, so by the time the decision was made there was working evidence about what per-level analysis actually feels like — and (a) turned out to be a subset of (c) rather than a rival to it. Deciding on day one would have been a guess; deciding after building the cheap half was a choice with evidence behind it. WHY (c) OVER (b), stated as the discriminator that survived from the brainstorm: every seam between designs costs a coordinate, an evidence roll-up and a freshness check, so a level earns its own graph only when it is separately owned, released or shared. A three-level tower of graphs inside one team pays all of that and buys none of it. (b) is not forbidden by this — a separately-owned system still gets its own design — it is that DEPTH stops being sufficient reason. WHAT THIS COSTS, recorded so nobody is surprised: docs/org-scale-vision.md's "one graph the whole company plans in" is now a road not taken, and req:concurrent-planning's answer changes shape — ownership boundaries become the primary isolation mechanism, with the claims layer and the merge driver serving work INSIDE one boundary rather than across all of them. The first rung built on this decision is the coordinate (cap:mirror-surface): the other side's published surface mirrored as local nodes carrying which design, which hash, and when.

properties.decision: UNDECIDED, and it is Anthony's call. The schema declares BOTH `SUPERSEDES` and `OBSOLETES` for the same relationship — one node retiring another on the record — and NEITHER is read by any computation. The choice is which one is the real vocabulary, and then making it mean something. Option A: keep `OBSOLETES` (the one the code and the retire-from-design skill already use) and delete `SUPERSEDES` from the schema and from docs/three-axes.md. Option B: keep `SUPERSEDES` (the one the schema's own doc comment describes as "target retired on the record") and migrate the code. Option C: both survive with a stated distinction — but nobody has yet said what that distinction would be, and two words for one relationship is how a vocabulary rots.
properties.name: OPEN — retirement is two edge types and neither is consulted: which one survives?
properties.rationale:
FOUND BY THE SCHEMA SWEEP, 2026-07-28, and it is the `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` shape at edge level rather than property level.

WHAT WAS MEASURED. `SUPERSEDES` has ZERO references in the entire Rust source: nothing creates it, nothing reads it. It is nonetheless documented in `nodes.rs` ("source supersedes target — target retired on the record") and named in `docs/three-axes.md` as part of what covers the time axis. `OBSOLETES` is the one actually in use — `collapse_decision` draws it when a chosen alternative retires the losers, and the retire-from-design skill instructs users to draw it for a capability or component with a successor. But `OBSOLETES` has NO READER either: grep across the whole core crate finds the constant, the one create site, and a doc comment. No rollup, detector or report consults it.

WHAT THAT MEANS TODAY, stated exactly rather than dramatised: retiring something marks it and changes nothing downstream. A retired capability still counts in every rollup, still raises its gaps, still appears in delivery arithmetic. It is currently LATENT — reflow2's own design contains zero instances of either edge, so the retire path has never been exercised on this project — but the skill is actively telling users to draw an edge that has no effect, which is worse than an edge nobody knows about.

WHY IT IS NOT JUST HOUSEKEEPING. `req:intent-preserved` ("the past is never overwritten") is the requirement retirement serves, and the retire-from-design skill exists precisely to force the question "was this ever true?" — history retired on the record versus a mistake deleted. That whole discipline currently terminates in an edge nothing reads. Whichever edge survives, the deciding question is the same: what SHOULD consult it — delivery roll-up, the gap detectors, `graph_report`'s counts — and does a retired node stop counting, or count separately?

DELIBERATELY LEFT `proposed`: this is a vocabulary choice with migration consequences for anyone who already drew either edge, and `dec:certainty-derived` forbids recording it as settled on the user's behalf.

properties.decision: single_point_of_failure candidates are Components, Interfaces, Resources, Environments.
properties.name: Only things that operate can be single points of failure
properties.rationale: The suggested fix is add_redundancy, and redundancy is only coherent for running parts; a golden thread converges on intent by design, so intent hubs are the thread working. 22 of 22 false positives cleared, 4 true survivors. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); BL-5.

properties.decision:
OPEN — Anthony's word needed. Anthony described the role as an attribute of each NODE in an architecture (publish / subscribe / both / non_external). reflow2 already carries something very close: `Interface.designation` (internal | published), with PROVIDES and CONSUMES naming who stands on which side. So the question is whether the pairing role extends the Interface, or becomes a property every node type carries.

ALTERNATIVES WEIGHED. (1) Extend `Interface.designation` — RECOMMENDED. (2) A role property on every node, Anthony's original shape: most general, lets any node participate in a seam; costs correctness, because a Component both publishes and subscribes so the value collapses to `both` and pairs with everything, and it adds a property to 28 node types for a case nothing currently needs. (3) Neither — keep pairing manual as mirror_surface does today and let compose_and_analyse surface a bad seam as an ordinary gap once a human has wired the two sides; cheapest, but leaves exactly the hand-wiring that made this idea worth having.
properties.name: Where the publish/subscribe role lives: on the Interface, or on every node
properties.rationale:
WHY THE INTERFACE. An Interface IS a boundary — it is the one node type whose entire reason for existing is to be the place two things meet, which is exactly what pairs. The publish side already exists there, is already exported by export_surface, and already withholds internals correctly. And a role is not intrinsic to a node: the same Component publishes one contract and subscribes to another, so a single role on the Component would be wrong about half the time. Anthony's `both` value is the tell — it is needed only because the attribute is sitting on the wrong noun. On an Interface, `both` is rare and meaningful (a genuinely bidirectional contract) rather than a shrug.

WHAT MUST BE ADDED WHICHEVER WAY IT GOES, because this is the actual missing half: a way to declare what a design NEEDS from outside — a REQUIRED boundary — standing on its own, without the consumer first having modelled the provider's contract inside its own design. Concretely, a third value alongside `internal` and `published`, plus the matchable KEY Anthony named (an id and a description), which is what one design's `required` is matched against another's `published`. Without a key, pairing falls back to fuzzy name matching alone, and names are exactly what two organisations that never coordinated will have chosen differently.

NOT SETTLED HERE: how a pair is recorded — an edge between the two Interfaces, or mirroring one into the other. MIRRORS already exists for the second; there is no edge type meaning "these two boundaries are the same boundary seen from opposite sides", and adding one WOULD move the version stamp and lock out older reflow2 installs.

properties.decision: Parallel alternatives (an analysis of alternatives held open until a decision) are represented BRANCH-BY-FILE: each alternative is a separate exported design (a git branch's reflow2.json, or an export file), not a world-tag inside one live graph. This reuses everything BL-80 built — cross-branch comparison is compare_designs, collapsing the winner is merge_designs/apply_merge, retiring the loser is retire-from-design — so reflow2 owns almost no new branch machinery, consistent with the merge's 'git is the DAG' decision. Semantically, alternatives are design SPACE, not time: sibling alternatives coexist 'now' and CONTRADICT each other, held under a proposed Decision (the decision point) until it collapses — distinct from an epoch (EVOLVES_INTO, before->after). Forking is not advancing time; storage may still be a ref/epoch, but the semantic layer keeps 'the road not taken' apart from 'an earlier version' (BL-70's warning). v1 is the N-way AoA report (analyze_alternatives): measures per branch (graph_report snapshot — nodes, open gaps, allocation health, verification coverage) side by side, plus each branch's structural divergence from a named baseline (compare_designs). Rung 2 wires the decision point: a proposed Decision GOVERNS lightweight alternative pointers that CONTRADICT their siblings; collapsing accepts the Decision, merges the winner into the baseline, and retires the losers with their rationale.
properties.name: AoA alternatives are branch-by-file and live in design-space (CONTRADICTS), not time (epochs)
properties.rationale: User decided both axes 2026-07-22, each the recommended option. Branch-by-file over world-scope because BL-80 already built the comparison (compare_designs), the collapse (merge/apply_merge) and the retire machinery, so branch-by-file is the cheapest increment BL-70 itself named ('one exported graph per alternative plus a cross-export comparison report ... branch-by-file works today') and it is consistent with dec:merge-three-way's 'explicit inputs, git is the DAG'; world-scoping would bake world-awareness into every detector (possible_duplicate, allocation, SPOF, …) — a large invasive change for a simultaneous-in-one-graph benefit not yet needed, and BL-70 says branch-by-file 'teaches what the real scoping primitive must preserve' first. Space-over-time because an AoA holds both roads at once (design space, CONTRADICTS); reusing the epoch/PRECEDES time chain for branches (git's literal branch=commit-in-a-DAG, BL-80 #3) would make the road-not-taken indistinguishable from an earlier version — exactly the conflation BL-70 warns against. This is the fork/navigation substrate BL-81 (roads-not-taken) needs and shares the scoping primitive with BL-44 (cluster claims). Deferred: the decision-point pointer nodes + collapse wiring (rung 2), world-scoping if simultaneous in-graph AoA proves needed, and per-branch readiness scoring (BL-68).

properties.decision: verification_coverage counts passing checks; a failing check is its own 0.8 gap.
properties.name: Verified means a check that passes, not one that exists
properties.rationale: A failing test used to satisfy the gap that asked for a test, and passing vs failing were byte-identical to every diagnostic — counting test nodes while ignoring test results. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); evidence: phase-coverage trial, BL-30.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. The one place the vocabulary genuinely strains against a plan. reflow2's temporal axis is DECISION time — DesignEpoch, Snapshot, valid_from/valid_to, ChangeEvent: "when did we settle this, and what was in force then". A plan needs EXECUTION time: H-hour and offsets from it, durations, windows, and a critical path computed from dependencies. Flow + PRECEDES + TRIGGERS gives ordering, not schedule. (a) ADD IT — scheduled instants/durations on Flow steps plus a computed critical path; the biggest vocabulary addition since the temporal axis, and it makes "the timeline slipped" a computation rather than a note. (b) LEAVE IT OUT and reference an external schedule (MS Project, a synch matrix) from the graph; keeps reflow2 out of a crowded, well-solved problem, at the cost that the blast radius of a slip cannot be computed — which is exactly the thing worth having. (c) MINIMAL — offsets from a named reference event and durations, no calendar, no resource levelling, no Gantt: enough to compute what a slip breaks, not enough to be a scheduling tool. THE VOCABULARY CONSTRAINT EITHER WAY: no military or acquisition words enter the schema (req:design-anything, and the way dec:mosa-conformance was settled) — H-hour is a named reference event, not a schema noun.
properties.name: OPEN — does reflow2 model scheduled time (H-hour, durations, critical path) as a first-class axis?
properties.rationale: Named as the honest gap while mapping a staff planning process onto the existing vocabulary, which otherwise carried it almost without strain: ALLOCATED_TO is troop-to-task, Interface plus PROVIDES/CONSUMES is a coordination point or transfer of authority, Decision plus register_alternative is COA development and comparison, Constraint is constraints and restraints with breach computed, Verification is a rehearsal or confirmation brief, and a FRAGO is a ChangeEvent with a computed blast radius. Recorded rather than acted on because (c) is a real design choice that turns on whether any computation would read it — the same test dec:exploratory-staging applies to brainstorm vocabulary — and because getting it wrong means either reimplementing MS Project badly or leaving the highest-value computation on the table. Detail in docs/planning-at-scale.md §1.

properties.decision: RESOLVED 2026-07-24 on Anthony's word: OPTION C. A read carries a loop-debt pointer ONLY when loop_status would report real outstanding debt, and stays silent when the loop is clean — never the static-every-read of (B), which BL-90 already rejected as boilerplate the agent learns to skim. AXIS 2 resolved: the hint rides the orientation-shaped reads (graph_report, scan_nodes, search_design, get_node — what an agent runs to get its bearings), and fires only when the owed-set CHANGES since it was last surfaced (fire-on-change) — so it appears once when debt arises and stays quiet until the picture moves, which also bounds the per-read cost of computing what is owed. The read-side sibling of the write tools' loop_hint (dec:loop-status-state-not-history). Satisfies req:read-surfaces-debt; unbuilt until it lands in the MCP read tools' result path. Options weighed: (A) do nothing — SessionStart + Stop suffice; (B) static reminder on every read; (C, CHOSEN) state-derived conditional hint.
properties.name: Reads surface loop debt only when it's real — option C (state-derived, orientation reads, fire-on-change)
properties.rationale: Leaning C on axis 1, for reasons already on the record. (B) is the failure mode the user explicitly rejected in BL-90 ("aggressive wording across ~90 tool descriptions — cancels out at that scale"): boilerplate on every return trains the agent to skim past it, and reads differ from writes in a way that makes static wrong here — a write always advances the loop (it creates debt, so a static "next step" is always relevant, which is why the write-side loop_hint is static and accepted), whereas a read creates no debt, so a constant reminder is irrelevant most of the time and becomes noise. (C) respects dec:loop-status-state-not-history (debt is computed from current state, never remembered) and dec:anchored-first (a real, named problem outranks a generic nudge). (A) is the honest null option: the three existing triggers may already be enough, and the marginal value of C is specifically the mid-session read that SessionStart and Stop don't see. Axis 2 exists because loop_status is cheap but not free; the throttle is where C's cost is paid. Sibling of the write-side loop_hint; BL-74 family. Awaits the user's word on both axes before anything is built to satisfy req:read-surfaces-debt.

properties.decision: DECIDED (a) READ-ONLY AT OPEN, on Anthony's word 2026-07-26: `open_cf_descriptors_read_only` — a consistent view as of the moment of opening. No lock, no secondary directory, nothing to clean up; seeing newer writes means reopening, which is cheap and explicit. (b) SECONDARY (`open_cf_as_secondary` + `try_catch_up_with_primary`) was rejected, not unconsidered: it refreshes on demand but needs its OWN directory for private state — the same class of thing as --export-snapshot's scratch dir, which has already bitten twice (a leaked sidecar, and a residue test that stripped only the suffix it knew about) — and StorageEngine's read cache could serve a value cached before a catch-up, stale in a way the caller cannot see. THE INTERACTION THAT DECIDED IT is with req:stale-seat-knows: (a) makes staleness BOUNDED AND KNOWABLE, so a read-only seat can state exactly how old its view is, which is the same property the export refusal just bought; (b) makes staleness fixable but turns 'how stale am I right now?' into a live question the seat must keep answering, which is the complete-but-older trap arriving from a new direction.
properties.name: A locked-out seat gets a read-only view as of open, not a catchable-up secondary
properties.rationale: Scoped 2026-07-26 by reading dynograph-foundation and tantivy rather than from memory, and the scoping changed the shape of the work: it is THREE crates, not one. FIRST UNKNOWN NOW CLOSED BY MEASUREMENT, not by documentation: two separate reader processes open and search a tantivy index while a third holds a live writer, the writer keeps working afterwards, and a second WRITER is still refused (crates/dynograph-text/tests/readers_beside_a_writer.rs, the first integration test that crate has had). Tantivy's own source claimed this was supported; nothing had ever done it, and a whole feature was about to be built on the claim. The reflow2 layer adds a third blocker of its own: reindex_search runs on EVERY server start and is a write.

properties.decision: When a past decision is re-opened to take a different road, the original Decision stays `accepted` untouched, and a NEW `proposed` Decision is created that OBSOLETES it and holds the alternatives (including the road originally taken, now a sibling rather than the incumbent). The decision-point machinery already built (register_alternative / alternatives_for / collapse_decision, and the undecided_decision_point gap) applies unchanged to the new node, because it is a genuinely open choice. The record therefore shows both that the question was settled and that it was later re-asked, with the reasoning of each visible in its own node.
properties.name: Re-opening a settled choice mints a new Decision that obsoletes the old one; the accepted Decision is never un-accepted
properties.rationale: User decided 2026-07-24. THE REJECTED ALTERNATIVE: flip the original Decision's status back to `proposed` and hang the new alternatives on it — simpler, and reuses the existing node. Rejected because it overwrites the fact that the choice was ever settled: a reader of the graph afterwards sees an open question and cannot tell it was once answered, or when, or on what grounds. That is the ADR failure mode this whole system was built against (dec:two-sided-accept, "silent drift-accept does not exist"), and it would make the strongest evidence for re-opening — that we chose X, lived with it, and the trials found the hole — the very thing the re-opening erases. Snapshots would in principle preserve it, but only if one was taken, which makes the integrity of the record contingent on remembering a second step. Superseding is unconditional. It also composes with the existing vocabulary rather than straining it: OBSOLETES already means "retired on the record, not deleted" (the retire-from-design exit), and the new node's own `alternatives` obituary is written by collapse_decision when the re-opened choice closes, so the second decision documents the first without rewriting it.

properties.decision: RocksDB directory beside the repo, exports as the durable, diffable record.
properties.name: The graph lives as a repo file, embedded — not a service
properties.rationale: The service's strongest argument (concurrency) is hypothetical while there is one writer; it would put the user's design on a machine they do not control and is permanent operational cost. Reopening conditions are written down. Decided 2026-07-18 (surface-plan.md); BL-12/BL-15 carry the consequences.

properties.decision: Per capability: drifting / confirmed / unexamined, with the disposition counts visible.
properties.name: The confirmation ledger reports claim history, never judges a claim
properties.rationale: Five design_holds claims with zero design edits is the erosion signature and the ledger makes it legible — but judging a specific claim false is semantic, and a deterministic detector would fire on every stable design with cosmetic churn (the unexpected_coupling lesson). Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); BL-35.

properties.decision: ACCEPT the single_point_of_failure finding on cmp:ingest rather than add redundancy. The topology it reports is true: cmp:sanitize is reached only through cmp:ingest today, because INGEST is the only path by which foreign text currently enters the graph, so every route to the trust boundary runs through one component.
properties.name: The trust boundary having one caller makes ingest an articulation point — accepted, and the fix is the second caller
properties.rationale: Recorded because the finding appeared the moment the sanitizer landed (2026-07-25) and would otherwise be re-litigated every session, and because the suggested fix is the wrong shape here: `add_redundancy` is coherent for a running part that can fail over, and a second copy of a pure text filter would be duplication, not resilience. What WILL dissolve it is already named in the module docs and in cap:sanitize-ingress — the import path. `import_graph` deliberately does not rewrite the document it is handed (an export's content is its identity), so the next rung is detect-and-report on import, and when that lands the boundary has two callers and the articulation point is gone honestly. Deliberately NOT done: wiring cmp:export or cmp:graph to cmp:sanitize now to quiet the detector, because that would be an edge the code does not have — the same fabrication dec:ask-not-repair forbids of a heuristic. Joins the five accepted SPOFs under the BL-93 disposition: loop_status will not call the structural set clean, and that is expected.

properties.decision: cmp:service is the sole bridge between the reflow2-mcp subsystem and both the core and the kit, and it stays that way. The single_point_of_failure warning on it is accepted as intentional, not resolved by adding redundancy.
properties.name: The single MCP service is an accepted single point of failure
properties.rationale: req:invocation mandates one reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio as the entire user-facing surface; a redundant second service would contradict that 'one door' design and buys nothing while there is a single local writer (dec:repo-file-embedded). Articulation-point analysis of the component/interface dependency graph (2026-07-21 self-host review) confirms cmp:service is a genuine cut vertex — removing it disconnects the MCP surface — so the finding is true, and the right disposition is to accept it rather than fix it. Contrast cmp:flow, flagged by the same detector but NOT a cut vertex (BL-69). Redundancy is the wrong fix; this SPOF is the architecture working as intended.

properties.decision: THE HARD CONSTRAINT FIRST, because it rules out the literal proposal: no harness discovers skills from an MCP server. Claude Code, OpenCode and Copilot read `.claude/skills/`, Grok CLI reads `.grok/skills/` (docs/skills/README.md), and a skill that is not in one of those directories is not a skill — it is a file nobody loads. So "reference something in the MCP to discover all those skills" cannot be honoured as harness-native skills today. What CAN be honoured is the substance: nothing in the project changes after setup, and updates ride the package. FOUR PIECES, separable, in increasing cost. (1) SERVER INSTRUCTIONS — already how reflow2 delivers its loop doctrine (the paragraph in every session's context comes from the server, versioned with the binary, zero repo files). The catalogue of skills, one line each, belongs here: that is exactly what a skill's frontmatter description does, and it is what makes progressive disclosure work. (2) A `reflow2_skill(name)` TOOL returning the body on demand, with `list_skills` alongside. Works in EVERY MCP client including Grok, needs no filesystem copy, and always matches the binary. (3) MCP PROMPTS — reflow2 declares only `enable_tools()`; adding `enable_prompts()` would serve the command-shaped skills as `/mcp__reflow2__<name>` slash commands with zero files in the repo. Claude-Code-shaped, so it complements (2) rather than replacing it. (4) LOCAL OVERRIDE — a skill present in the project's own `.claude/skills/` wins over the served one, so customisation survives and the served set is a default rather than a cage. WHAT THE PROJECT WOULD STILL HOLD after all four: the pointer paragraph, `.mcp.json` (and the other harnesses' formats), `.reflow2/` and its gitignore line. That is his brother's proposal exactly.
properties.name: OPEN — do the skills come from the server instead of being copied into the project?
properties.rationale: Feedback from Anthony's brother, 2026-07-25, and it names the same failure shape reflow2 keeps finding in itself: a COPY drifts, and the fix is to remove the copying rather than to refresh it better — the same reasoning that retired the fleet's mint-race guard in dec:identity-out-of-band, and the same one behind computed-not-remembered everywhere else in this project. The evidence is already on the record: the installer's docstring concedes that the kit freezes while reflow2 moves, and reflow2's OWN kit manifest went four releases stale with nothing noticing. THE HONEST COST, recorded beside the idea: a harness-native skill is auto-matched by the harness from its description without the agent being asked, and a served skill is not — the agent has to know to call for it. Moving skills to the server therefore trades the harness's own progressive disclosure for freshness, and the mitigation (the catalogue in the server instructions) is a hand-built version of what the harness does for free. That trade is the decision, and it is worth putting to both brothers rather than assuming: one of them is the consumer whose repo churns, the other is the one who would maintain two delivery paths.

properties.decision: Every epoch on the retrospective chain corresponds to a real shipped release with a real git tag and date (v0.4.0 through v0.10.1), plus the pre-existing genesis and post-v0.5.0-hardening epochs. Each Decision is anchored to the epoch of the earliest release whose committed export actually contains it — evidence from the repo, not reconstruction from memory. Each Release is pinned to its own epoch. Epochs before v0.9.0 carry no checksum, because their exports predate the hash chain; they say so in their description rather than claiming one. Going forward, an epoch is cut as work happens so nothing needs backfilling again.
properties.name: The epoch chain is backfilled from shipped releases only — real tags, or nothing
properties.rationale: User decided 2026-07-24 among three options. THE REJECTED ALTERNATIVES: (a) forward-only — anchor from today and leave the past alone. Rejected because all 34 existing decisions are the ones actually worth re-opening; a fork layer that can only fork decisions made after it was built is a fork layer with nothing to fork. (b) full reconstruction — invent an epoch per work session across the whole history and synthesize the missing snapshots. Rejected because most of those boundaries are guesses, and a fabricated epoch is worse than an absent one: it looks like evidence. Release tags are the natural resolution because they are the only points in this project's history that are independently attested (a tag, a date, a published binary, a committed export), and because "the design as of the release that shipped it" is the question a fork actually asks. The cost is deliberately accepted: the 9 founding decisions anchor to v0.4.0, the earliest tag carrying an export, which is their earliest EVIDENCE rather than their origin — recorded as such in that epoch's description instead of being silently presented as the date they were made. FOUND WHILE DOING THIS: reflow2's own temporal axis was nearly unused — zero Snapshots, 8 of 42 ChangeEvents pinned, no Decision anchored at all, the chain stopped four days back — because add_change_event (cheap, epoch-free) had been used throughout where record_change (pins and snapshots) was meant. The fork layer's foundation was missing, not merely its ref layer.

properties.decision: Every capability is designed as a check one party places on another; none does another's job.
properties.name: The LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides
properties.rationale: The parties are not interchangeable: the LLM cannot be trusted with arithmetic, memory or its own confidence; the graph cannot judge meaning; the human cannot remember everything or notice slow drift. The deterministic core computes, the graph carries claims and their audit trail, questions route judgment to the human. docs/partnership.md maps each known LLM failure mode to its mechanism. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam).

properties.decision: set_artifact_checksum requires a disposition: design_holds (a dated claim) or design_updated (naming the design-side ChangeEvent, linked to the artifact).
properties.name: Silent drift-accept does not exist
properties.rationale: 'Accept the file, leave the design alone, say nothing' is how a design erodes into fiction over N legitimate fix cycles while reporting zero gaps — the failure that sank the original reflow. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); evidence: erosion trials, BL-33.

properties.decision: DECIDED on Anthony's word, 2026-07-26: "go with freshness fact on the confirmation ledger (always visible, never nagging)". The alternative was a gap source — asked once through gap_to_prompt, acknowledgeable, and appearing in detect_gaps until answered. Rejected for the reason the ledger's own module doc already gives about signals: a stale-looking check is a STANDING PROPERTY of a claim rather than an event, it would fire on every legitimate refactor as readily as on a real hole, and an open list that can never reach zero gets skimmed — which is precisely the failure the gap workflow exists to prevent (the BL-23 lesson: when a detector punishes correct work, the answer is a different question, not a tuned threshold). As a ledger fact it is visible every time somebody asks how a claim stands, and it nags nobody.
properties.name: A check older than its code is a freshness FACT, not a gap
properties.rationale: Prompted by a real miss the same day. cap:degraded-surface was `verified` with a passing check, and that check drove stdio only; adding the HTTP transport widened what "the server explains its own absence" had to mean, without widening anything that tested it. reflow2 reported zero gaps throughout, and it was right to — nothing it knew was false. But it HAD the evidence: art:main drifted twice (chg:shared-sessions, chg:remote-sessions) while art:test-degraded-server never moved, and Verification.last_run_at is written by verify.rs and read by nothing anywhere in the core. Same shape this project keeps finding — a field declared, written, and consulted by no computation (the temporal axis before BL-70, the whole inviolable-intent vocabulary before BL-96): the higher-yield question is what the core already does that nothing can reach. Deliberately NOT the wider question of measuring what a check actually covers, which is unknowable from the graph and belongs to BL-95.

properties.decision: Renderers may only emit what the graph states; everything else is confessed as a finding.
properties.name: A view is a projection of the graph; renderer fill-ins are defects
properties.rationale: UAF/DoDAF doctrine from the author: the graph stores all design detail, the agent only renders viewpoints. If rendering requires extrapolation, something is missing inside reflow2 — almost always. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); render_views.py, BL-40.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. When a plan moves during execution — "the motorcade slips thirty minutes" — somebody has to be told, and the question is who decides that. (a) SUBSCRIPTION, the way every coordination tool works: you join a channel, or somebody remembers to include you on the distribution. Cheap, familiar, and it fails one way every time — the person who most needed to know was not on the list, and nobody finds out until it matters. (b) DERIVED FROM THE BLAST RADIUS: propagate_from already returns who a change impacts, including which published boundaries it crosses, so the owners of the impacted regions ARE the distribution. Nobody maintains a list, nobody is spammed with changes that cannot touch them, and when the plan changes shape the distribution changes with it for free. (c) BOTH — derived by default, with an explicit watch for people who want a region they do not own. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT TO (b), recorded beside it: a blast radius is only as good as the edges that exist, so an unrecorded dependency means a silent non-notification — which is the same failure as (a), reached by a different route, and arguably harder to notice because the mechanism looks principled. The mitigation is that a missing edge is already what detect_gaps hunts, so the honesty debt has an owner.
properties.name: OPEN — is notification computed from the blast radius, or subscribed to?
properties.rationale: This is the most distinctive idea in the 1000-planner exploration and the strongest reason reflow2 would belong in that problem rather than a chat tool with a plan attached: a FRAGO is a ChangeEvent whose blast radius is computed, and "who does this break" is a question reflow2 already answers. It is the same shape as every other answer in this project — computed, not remembered — and it inherits the honesty rules, so a notification would have to say what changed, what it impacts and what is now unresolved, never "the plan was updated". Kept separate from dec:live-tier because the mechanism choice is separable: (b) is worth building for a single team on the repo-file architecture, with no hosting at all, the moment anyone wants it.

properties.statement: Anthony's reframe, 2026-07-25, of what to do with the GitHub-MCP study's larger lessons: rather than hold them as a roadmap of features to build, hold them as a rule about what NOT to do now — do not take a shortcut today that would make it impossible for reflow2 to become what GitHub's MCP server is. A roadmap ages badly and gets stale in a document nobody reads; a non-foreclosure rule is checkable at the moment of the decision that would break it, which is the only moment it matters. THE SPECIFIC FORECLOSURES, from reading github-mcp-server (each one a shortcut that is tempting precisely because there is one writer today): (1) IDENTITY IN A GLOBAL. Authority must arrive with the caller and be read from the request, never stashed in a process-wide variable or resolved once at startup — GitHub constructs a fresh server per request in stateless mode for exactly this reason, and their lockdown cache carries the warning that a viewer-scoped lookup shared across requests runs under the wrong user's credentials. (2) INVENTING AUTHORITY. reflow2 must never become the thing that decides who may read what; it delegates to an authority that already exists, on GitHub's stated principle that a server must not let anyone reach more than they could reach without it. Building an account system would foreclose that by making reflow2 the authority. (3) TREATING THE SINGLE-WRITER LOCK AS A CONTRACT. One RocksDB handle is an implementation fact; the day it is a promise in a tool description or a skill, concurrency becomes a breaking change rather than a build. (4) CONFIG THAT WIDENS. Per-request configuration must only ever NARROW what the deployment allowed — GitHub's headers can restrict within static bounds and can never re-include what was excluded, and any read-only surface that a header can talk out of read-only was never read-only. (5) ONE GRAPH ASSUMED EVERYWHERE. graph_id already exists on every node and edge and is pinned to a constant; code that assumes the constant rather than reading the field is the foreclosure, not the constant itself. (6) TRUSTING TEXT BY ITS LOCATION. Once a design can arrive from someone else, text is untrusted because of where it came from, not because of which field it sits in — so the trust boundary belongs at ingress, before anything reads it. WHAT THIS RULE IS NOT: it is not a licence to build the hosted service, and not a reason to add abstraction now. Every item above is a constraint on shortcuts, satisfiable by writing the simple version carefully — the point is that the simple version stays a strict subset of the eventual one, so nothing has to be undone. ENFORCEMENT DECIDED 2026-07-25 (Anthony: "go with your recommendation"): ADVISORY, `enforced: false`, and deliberately so. VIOLATES_RULE is a vocabulary item no detector reads, so declaring this gate-blocking would promise a check that does not exist — the exact failure the KPP work was built to end ("a KPP that nothing checks is a comment"). The rule is the project's rule, confirmed by its author; the flag says only that no build has been stopped by it yet. It flips to enforced the day a detector can read a foreclosure from graph state — the honest first candidate being (4) and (5), which are mechanically checkable, unlike (2), which is a judgement about architecture.

properties.spec: Corrected 2026-07-28: this claimed `medium: REST` because REST was the schema default, and it is a Rust library API linked directly by callers — no transport, no wire, no endpoint. The false value was never chosen by anyone; it arrived by default.

properties.name: Design export document
properties.spec: Corrected 2026-07-28: claimed `medium: REST` by default. It is a JSON document written to a path and read back — a data contract, not a network one. Its shape is the export schema (nodes, edges, graph_id, stamp, content_hash, prev_content_hash).

properties.name: MCP tool surface
properties.spec: MEDIUM IS KNOWN-WRONG AND THE CORRECTION IS OWED. `REST` here was never chosen — it arrived as the schema default, which was changed to `unspecified` on 2026-07-28 (req:seam-incompatibility) precisely because a default must not assert a technology. This value could not be corrected in the same session: the live MCP server is the binary from session start and its schema predates the new enum value, so it refused the write. Fix after an /mcp reconnect. AND THE VOCABULARY HAS NO RIGHT ANSWER YET, which is the more interesting half: MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0 carried over EITHER a stdio pipe to a launched process OR streamable HTTP, and reflow2 serves both from one surface. `REST` is wrong (not resource-oriented; the HTTP transport is a single endpoint), `cli` is wrong for the HTTP case, `gRPC` is a different protocol. The enum wants `json_rpc`, or a way for one contract to name two media. Raised for Anthony rather than guessed: inventing schema vocabulary is a design decision, and asserting a wrong-but-plausible value is the exact failure that produced this whole correction.

properties.answer: Anthony, 2026-07-27: "go with your recommendation: the interface." Recorded as `dec:pairing-role-placement` (accepted) and `req:complementary-pairing` moved to accepted. The role extends `Interface.designation` rather than becoming a per-node attribute — a Component both publishes and subscribes, so a per-node role collapses to `both` and pairs with everything. AMENDED 2026-07-28 after the dynograph-foundation trial refuted the first draft of the matching key: base-compatibility is `medium` PLUS `transport_security` PLUS `auth`, because role-plus-medium alone would pair a consumer requiring REST against a public unauthenticated liveness probe. The gap stays open because the requirement is accepted but NOT YET BUILT — that is the honest state, not an unanswered question.

properties.question: Does the publish/subscribe role belong on the interface itself — extending the `published` flag with a third value meaning "I need one of these from outside" — or on every node, as you described it? Recommendation: the interface. A component both publishes and subscribes, so a single role on a component collapses to `both` and pairs with everything, which is the only reason `both` is needed at all. On an interface, `both` stays rare and means something real.

properties.answer: Anthony, 2026-07-28: "go ahead with req:seam-incompatibility". BUILT as `seam_report`. Compares paired boundaries across eight axes — medium, paradigm, payload_format, auth, transport_security, operations, error_model, payload_schema — and classifies each as agreed / incompatible / differs / unstated. Three rules, all from what the trial established: `unspecified` on either side is UNSTATED and never agreement, so "0 incompatibilities" can never be read as compatible; free-text axes report as DIFFERS for a person, never as incompatible, because a machine cannot tell a real mismatch from different wording; and the report always names what it did NOT examine (con:pairing-stops-at-the-boundary — the types that CROSS a boundary are invisible to it). Pairing is supplied rather than computed, because the subscribe side is not declarable until req:complementary-pairing lands.
properties.context_setter: Nothing satisfies requirement “When two linked designs disagree at a seam, say so”
properties.question: reflow2 can tell you when a connection between two projects is missing a side, but not when both sides exist and simply disagree — one sending a format the other does not expect, or one assuming a speed the other cannot meet. That is the failure that survives testing until it does not. Do you want reflow2 to catch that, knowing it only works once the connection details above are captured properly?

properties.answer: Anthony, 2026-07-28: build it, derived from build files rather than hand-authored. BUILT. `reflow2.toml` is generated from declarations held in the graph and carries which reflow2 wrote it (his earlier ask). Two facts are kept apart deliberately: what you MEAN to depend on (the declaration, durable and committed) and what your build ACTUALLY resolves (the observation, read fresh each time) — storing only the first gives a document that drifts, storing only the second gives a fact nothing can contradict. `reconcile_dependencies` compares them and catches both opposite failures. Core does not parse Cargo.toml: the caller supplies the observation, as `reconcile_artifacts` and `coverage_report` already do, because storyflow pins one dependency across a Cargo.toml, a docker-compose.yml and a versions.env, and a Cargo-only core would model a third of that seam and report the rest as absent.
properties.context_setter: Nothing satisfies requirement “Declare which version of another design you depend on, not just record what you took”
properties.question: reflow2 already notes which version of another project's design you actually copied, and when. What it has no place for is you SAYING which version you mean to depend on — a checked-in file like Cargo.toml. With both, it could tell you whether you are using the version you intended, and whether the other project has moved on since. Do you want that file, and should it come before or after the interface work?

properties.answer: Yes — build it. (Anthony, 2026-07-28: "go with req:publishable-promise next".) Built as the recommended option: a `designation` on Requirement mirroring the one on Interface, so a promise travels with the surface and every existing check applies to it unchanged, rather than a prose companion sitting outside all of them.
properties.context_setter: Nothing satisfies requirement “A published surface must be able to carry a behavioural promise, not only structure”
properties.question: When one project publishes what another may rely on, it can currently list the connection points but cannot state what any of them PROMISES to do. So dynograph's real commitment — that a missing database fails loudly rather than silently losing your data — has no way to reach the people depending on it, and today survives only as a comment in our own build file. Should I make a promise markable as publishable, so it travels with the surface and gets checked like everything else? This is my recommended next build: small, reuses machinery that already works, and until it exists every published surface reflow2 produces is missing half of what one is for.

properties.answer: "I believe documentation is part of reflow2 (not external to). I think that is true to just about any project deliverable — that documentation is part of the project. It'd be like if I designed a fighter jet using reflow2, but then didn't deliver any documentation on it to the user. Likewise, documentation is part of reflow2 itself." — Anthony, 2026-07-24. So documentation is owned by the product, not treated as material about it: a new Documentation subsystem containing a docs component now owns cap:explains-itself, and README.md and getting-started/SETUP.md are registered as checksummed Artifacts realizing it. The consequence he is asserting, taken literally: a README that drifts from what the system does is a detectable defect on the same footing as drifted code, not something someone eventually notices.
properties.context_setter: Capability “Explain itself to someone who has not been convinced yet” isn't assigned to any part
properties.question: You want reflow2 to explain plainly what it is and how to run it, before it explains what it believes. Nothing currently owns that job — the README, the getting-started guide and the diagrams are written by hand and belong to no part of the system. Should one part be responsible for explaining reflow2 to a newcomer, or is that simply documentation that lives outside the design?
