properties.name: v0.9.0
A system that already exists can be brought under design control
properties.statement: Requirements, functions and structure can be recovered from a running system.

properties.name: An agent can drive the whole loop
properties.statement: Every capability is reachable from a coding agent over one surface.

properties.name: Any level of the design can be analysed on its own, and a narrowed answer says what it left out
properties.statement: A person or team responsible for one part of a design must be able to point the detectors at that part and be answered about it — "is my subsystem coherent, what is it owed" — without reading the whole program. Anthony, 2026-07-25, from the satellite case: an organisation building a satellite capability has a space segment, a ground/user segment and a control segment; his team owns the satellite, and more specifically inter-satellite laser communications. He must understand the system of systems, but day to day he needs his own part. Two properties are inseparable from the first. A narrowed answer must NAME WHAT IT WITHHELD — findings elsewhere in the design, and findings that belong to no part in particular — because a team shown only its own corner will conclude the program is healthy, which is the silent-drop failure req:no-silent-fallback forbids, one level up from a truncated read. And narrowing must never become the tool deciding what a team is allowed to worry about: a program-level finding that touches their work still reaches them, marked as the program's rather than theirs. Deliberately silent on WHERE the levels live: a subtree of one graph and a design of its own are both answers to this, and that is the architecture question recorded as dec:nested-graphs.

properties.name: As-designed vs as-built divergence is detectable
properties.statement: Real files on disk are registered as checksummed Artifacts realizing capabilities, so drift between the design and the build is visible rather than assumed.

properties.name: A claim names its owner, and a claim with no live owner is reported stale
properties.statement: A claim records the session that made it (its harness session id — assigned out of band, so it cannot race), and claim_report distinguishes a claim held by a live seat from one left behind by a session that closed. Liveness is computed from the owner, not asserted by the claim: a claim nobody is working is a ghost that makes the overlap report lie.

properties.name: Design stays coherent across its lifecycle
properties.statement: When anything changes in any phase, the ripples are found and surfaced.

properties.name: Pair two designs by complementary role, so the seam is computed rather than hand-wired
properties.statement:
Anthony's idea (2026-07-27), and the analogy he reached for is load-bearing rather than decorative: RNA strands pair because the bases are COMPLEMENTARY — adenine with uracil, guanine with cytosine — never like-with-like. Applied here: each boundary declares a ROLE — it publishes, it subscribes, it does both, or it is not external at all — and each project publishes only its publish-or-both boundaries with an id and a description. Combining two designs then starts mechanically: match every publisher against every subscriber, associate them, and treat the pair as ONE graph for every ordinary reflow2 check — gaps, defects, god nodes, surprising connections. The pairing is what makes composition cheap; everything after it already exists (cap:composed-analysis).

DECIDED 2026-07-27 (dec:pairing-role-placement, accepted on Anthony's word): the role lives on the INTERFACE, extending `designation`, not on every node. A Component both publishes and subscribes, so a per-node role collapses to `both` and pairs with everything — the `both` value was the tell that the attribute was on the wrong noun.

WHAT REFLOW2 ALREADY HAS. `Interface.designation` is the publish flag (`internal | published`, defaulting to internal because publishing is a commitment). `export_surface` emits published Interfaces plus the Components either side and withholds the rest. `PROVIDES` and `CONSUMES` carry the two roles at the edge level. The publish half works end to end.

WHAT IS MISSING, and it is the whole idea: THE SUBSCRIBE SIDE IS NOT DECLARABLE. A design says what it OFFERS; it cannot say what it NEEDS from outside in a form another design can be matched against. Today a need is a CONSUMES edge pointing at an Interface the consumer modelled INSIDE ITS OWN design — so a match only happens where the consumer already guessed the provider's contract and named it compatibly. Without that half there is no complementary strand.

THREE OUTCOMES, ALL USEFUL: a publisher matched to a subscriber (the seam, computed); a publisher nobody subscribes to (dead surface); a subscriber nothing publishes (an unmet need — the loudest signal there is). Two publishers of one key is a fourth: a duplicated provider, a conflict rather than a match.

THE PAIRING KEY IS NOT NAME ALONE — AMENDED 2026-07-28 AFTER A REAL TRIAL. Complementary role plus a matching key was the first draft, and the dynograph-foundation session refuted it from the provider's side within an hour of the channel opening. Their design carries three `medium: REST` boundaries: `ifc:rest-v1` (TCP, JWT), `ifc:uds` (Unix socket, JWT, `transport_security: physical`) and `ifc:ops-probes` (PUBLIC AND UNAUTHENTICATED BY DESIGN, because an orchestrator's liveness check cannot hold a credential). Under role-plus-medium alone, a consumer declaring "I require REST" pairs against all three — including the unauthenticated probe surface. That is not a near-miss; it is the pairing rule confidently producing a wrong and security-relevant answer.

So base-compatibility is `medium` PLUS `transport_security` PLUS `auth`. Every one of those is already a property on Interface, put there by req:interface-spec-complete; the fault was leaving them out of the key, not a missing field. And the analogy survives the correction better than it started: adenine–uracil is two hydrogen bonds, guanine–cytosine three. COMPATIBILITY WAS NEVER A SINGLE POINT OF CONTACT.

A mismatch on those axes must be REPORTED AS AN INCOMPATIBILITY, never dropped as a non-match. "You publish this, I need this, and we cannot be connected the way either of us is built" is exactly the finding worth having, and silence would hide it.

NAMES ARE STILL FUZZY. `auth-api` against `AuthService` is the Bob/Bobby/Robert problem, already solved once: ingest's two-band resolution (below fuzzy_threshold = no match, between = a reported candidate, above auto_merge_threshold = act) plus the token-subset pass that catches `Gateway` vs `API Gateway`. Reuse that rather than inventing a second matcher, and ASK about the middle band (dec:ask-not-repair).

UNLABELLED MUST NOT READ AS `non_external`. A boundary nobody classified silently counting as internal means a design that never did the labelling pairs with nothing and reports a clean seam — the blindness cap:coverage exists to end. The pairing report must count and name what carries no role, as coverage_report does.

properties.name: Whether intent has been delivered is computed from the golden thread, never asserted
properties.statement: A requirement's completion must be derived from evidence already in the graph — something satisfies it, and that capability is realized and its check passes — not set by hand on the requirement itself. A hand-set "done" is a claim that outlives the truth: it survives the capability regressing, the artifact drifting, the verification starting to fail, and it degrades exactly as silently as an unreconciled checksum. Derived completion also makes the reverse question answerable without anyone maintaining it: what fraction of accepted intent is actually delivered, and which requirements are believed-done on evidence that no longer holds. The same rule applies to the rest of the lifecycle: a requirement that stopped being satisfied must be able to say so, rather than remaining green because nobody revisited it.

properties.name: Import one design into another and analyse the whole
properties.statement: reflow2 must be able to bring a dependency's design into a consuming design and run its ordinary analysis over the combined whole, so that composition problems appear as ordinary gaps rather than requiring a bespoke comparator. WHAT BLOCKS IT TODAY IS CONCRETE, not vague: import_graph writes every node under its ORIGINAL id with upsert semantics, so importing design Z into design A means Z's `cap:store` silently overwrites A's `cap:store`. It was built for layering a design onto itself — its own doc says an export can be layered onto a design it references — and using it to compose two DIFFERENT designs would corrupt the consumer without saying so. The other two composition mechanisms do not do this either, and it is worth being exact about why: mirror_surface deliberately imports only the published SURFACE and keeps it foreign, and merge_designs is a three-way merge of two versions of the SAME design. So a fourth thing is needed — a NAMESPACED import where both designs coexist and are separately identifiable. TWO THINGS THAT MUST NOT BE LOST. First, the combined graph must never be mistaken for the consumer's own design: every imported node stays attributable to where it came from, and an export of A must not start shipping Z's internals. Second, project-level detectors would now reason over both designs, so a consumer would see gaps belonging to its dependency — noise that would get the whole feature switched off. cap:scoped-analysis already narrows detection to a region and reports what it left out, so scoping the combined analysis to the seam is the likely answer rather than a new filter. NOTE THE TENSION WITH dec:nested-graphs, which chose a graph per ownership boundary precisely because edges cannot cross stores: this does not overturn that decision — the designs stay separately owned and separately released — but it does mean a THIRD, analysis-only composition alongside the two that exist.

properties.name: Several people can plan against one design without colliding
properties.statement: A team, not a single author, must be able to work on one design at the same time: each person able to see what the others hold, to work in a scope that does not collide with theirs, and to have genuinely overlapping work surfaced as decidable conflicts rather than silent last-writer-wins. Whether this extends to simultaneous editing with live presence, or stops at non-colliding parallel work with good merges, is deliberately not asserted here — it depends on an architecture question that is still open, and the weaker form may be what teams actually need.

properties.name: A whole corpus of existing specifications can be brought into the design in one pass
properties.statement: Where a system's intent already exists as a large body of written specifications, reflow2 must be able to take the whole corpus — a folder, not a file — and produce one coherent design from it, with every claim still pointing back at the document it came from. The load-bearing requirement is identity ACROSS documents: the same component named in forty specifications must converge on one node rather than forty near-duplicates, and where convergence is uncertain the user is asked rather than the nodes being silently merged. Ordering must not decide meaning — which file happened to be read first must not determine the canonical name of anything.

properties.name: The design must be able to say how much of the system it has never modelled
properties.statement: reflow2 must be able to report the portion of a real system that no node in the design has ever claimed, so that the thinness of a recovered or evolving model is measurable rather than merely felt. An empty gap list must mean "the design is coherent AND it covers the system", not "the design is coherent about the fraction it happens to know". The report says what is unclaimed and how large it is; it never scores the design, never blocks, and never treats coarse-but-honest modelling as a deficiency — a single opaque Component legitimately claims everything beneath it.

properties.name: Recording an open question must never assert that it was settled
properties.statement: A Decision's status must not be set on the user's behalf. Recording a choice someone is still facing — an open question, a brainstormed option, a decision point held for later — must land as `proposed`, and reaching `accepted` must be a separate, deliberate act. Found as friction 2026-07-25: add_decision defaults to `accepted`, so six open questions recorded in one session each landed as settled and needed correcting immediately afterwards. This generalises dec:certainty-derived from requirements to decisions, and the reason is the same: an accepted Decision is what where-am-i reads back to the user as "what you decided", what the fork layer treats as binding, and what the KPP contradiction check reads as a trade already made. A musing recorded as a reasoned choice is therefore worse than a missing record — it is a false one, attributed to them. Evidence it was systemic rather than one slip: the correction had become a standing note carried across sessions, and the brainstorm skill had to instruct it in prose ("this call is not optional"), which is a defect with a bandage on it.

properties.name: A default must not assert what nobody chose
properties.statement:
FOUND BY A DELIBERATE SWEEP, 2026-07-28, asking the question `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` implies but does not answer: what ELSE does the schema claim that no computation checks? The sweep was Anthony's call after the same defect shape appeared six times in three days.

THE MEASURED FINDING. Ten properties are materialised onto every node by the store's schema defaults and appear ZERO times in the entire Rust source — not in a detector, not in a report, not in a test. Measured against reflow2's own 860-node design:

- `Requirement.concern` — `core` on 67 of 67
- `Capability.tier` — `operational` on 84 of 84
- `Component.tier` — `operational` on 53 of 53
- `Capability.is_entry_point` / `is_exit_point` — `false` on 84 of 84
- `Constraint.concern`, `DesignRule.enforced`, `Actor.actor_type`, `EnvironmentRule.mandatory`, `EnvironmentRule.rule_type`, `Flow.tier` — likewise defaulted, likewise unread

Single-valued across the whole design, every one. A property that never varies is not carrying information; it is asserting one.

THE WORST INSTANCE, and the reason this is intent rather than tidiness. `Requirement.concern`'s enum is core / logistics / sustainment / safety / security / cost / schedule / manufacturability / usability / environmental — and the schema's own description says logistics and sustainment are there to carry "the ILS considerations an SME surfaces". That is the systems-engineering angle this project exists to serve, encoded in the schema and then asserted away: every requirement claims `core`, there is NO WRITER for it on the MCP surface (only the `create_node` escape hatch — the same shape as the KPP `objective` finding), and nothing reads it. So "which of these are the safety requirements?" cannot be answered, and the graph does not answer "unknown" — it answers "none".

THE RULE, AND IT IS ALREADY PROVEN HERE. `Interface.medium` defaulting to `REST` was fixed on 2026-07-28 for exactly this reason, and `ver:interface-spec` states the principle in the form it should now generalise: "UNRECORDED FIELDS READ AS `unspecified` NOT `none` — the flattering default would tell a consumer an unspecified contract is open." So: A DEFAULT MAY RECORD ABSENCE; IT MAY NOT RECORD A CHOICE. Where a property has a substantive default nobody selected, the default becomes `unspecified` and silence reads as silence.

WHY IT IS NOT MERELY COSMETIC. `export_surface` publishes a design's boundary to another design; a mirrored surface carrying `tier: operational` and `concern: core` ships assertions nobody made across a seam, which is the same failure `req:publishable-promise` was raised for one layer down. And the moment any future computation DOES read one of these — the SME view `concern` was designed for — it reads a value the schema invented.

THE COUNTERWEIGHT, and it is what stops this being a blanket rewrite: a default that records a genuine absence is CORRECT and must stay. `provenance: authored` and `status: proposed` are real defaults meaning a real thing. The test is whether the default names a CHOICE among alternatives (tier, concern, rule_type) or the ABSENCE of one — only the first kind lies. Changing a default is also not retroactive: nodes written before the change keep the value they were given, so a sweep of existing designs is a separate, deliberate act.

SIBLING FINDINGS FROM THE SAME SWEEP, recorded here rather than lost. (1) Fifteen properties are WRITTEN and never consulted — the sharpest is `DriftEvent.severity`, written from `kind.severity()` at three call sites while ranking independently re-derives it via `severity_rank(kind)`, so the stored copy can silently diverge from the mapping that actually governs; also `DesignEpoch.sequence`, which COORD entries quote as meaningful ("epoch:v0180 at sequence 210") and nothing orders by. (2) `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` is an instance of ITSELF: it carries `concern: core`, one of the properties nothing reads.

properties.name: Design anything, not only software
properties.statement: Software, hardware, a document, a process — the vocabulary stays neutral.

properties.name: A system's design can be a unit of its own that composes with the designs around it
properties.statement: Anthony, 2026-07-25, promoting the idea he had been thinking out loud about: "being able to have multiple repos that are linked by interface specifications (reflow2 could take both graphs and figure out how to resolve differences between those two repos to ensure they work together)... the idea would allow teams to focus in their most immediate concern and let the interface take care of how it works with all the other systems/components." The intent is that a design need not be one document for one program: a team owning a system can hold ITS design as a unit — its own store, its own lifecycle, its own published surface — and that unit composes with the systems around it through the interfaces between them, so the day-to-day view is genuinely local and the cross-system agreement is carried by the contract rather than by everyone reading everything. Four things follow, each a real obligation rather than a detail. The link between two designs cannot be an edge, because the schema validates both endpoints of every edge and they live in different stores; it must be a COORDINATE that names the other design, the node in it, and the version of it being built against. A parent's view of a composed child must ROLL UP the child's evidence — what it delivers and what it has proven — or a requirement satisfied inside the child fires as unsatisfied in the parent forever. That view is a dated claim about a VERSION of the child, never a live truth, so staleness is part of the model and not an afterthought. And the seam becomes the place where two teams genuinely collide, which is precisely where the merge machinery does not yet reach. This restates in the design what BL-45 recorded on 2026-07-20 from the same author, and it is deliberately silent on federation-versus-one-graph, which is dec:nested-graphs.

properties.name: Declare which version of another design you depend on, not just record what you took
properties.statement: A project that composes with another design must be able to DECLARE which version of it that dependency is on — a tag, a commit, a release — in a checked-in manifest a person edits, the way Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, pixi.toml or uv.toml declare code dependencies. Anthony's framing, 2026-07-27: when two projects evolve separately you need to know which version yours depended upon. WHAT ALREADY EXISTS IS THE OTHER HALF, and the distinction is the whole point. cap:mirror-surface already RECORDS the coordinate after the fact — mirror_content_hash is the content hash of the surface document a mirror was made from, and mirrored_at dates it, deliberately as a dated claim rather than a live truth. That is what you GOT. A manifest is what you MEANT: human-meaningful (v0.11.0, not a 64-character hash), authored rather than derived, reviewable in a diff, and readable before any graph is opened. HAVING BOTH IS WHAT MAKES THE CHECK POSSIBLE: declared-versus-mirrored answers 'am I actually composing against the version I said', and declared-versus-upstream answers 'has what I depend on moved since'. Either question is unanswerable with only one of the two halves. THE MANIFEST MUST ALSO RECORD WHICH REFLOW2 WROTE IT (Anthony, same day) — the same discipline the export stamp already follows, and for the same reason: a manifest is read by a binary that may be older or newer than the one that produced it, and a file that cannot say which vocabulary it was written against forces the reader to guess. reflow2 already refuses rather than guesses when an export's stamp is unreadable; the manifest should be no weaker. The manifest must also survive the case where the dependency's design is not available at all, because declaring a dependency you cannot currently resolve is a normal state and silence about it would be the failure.

properties.name: A durable design knows its own name, and remembers it across opens
properties.statement: A design that composes with others must have a stable identity of its own, remembered beside the store rather than supplied on each open. Found while building cap:mirror-surface on 2026-07-25: every reflow2 graph carried the same hardcoded graph_id, so no design could tell another design from itself — mirroring had to refuse a surface whose source id equalled its own, and with one constant that check could never pass. `open_in_memory_as` fixed it for library and test use; the durable case is unsolved and is deliberately not half-built, because the id namespaces every stored key: an on-disk graph reopened under a different name would find nothing, and one reopened under the DEFAULT name after being created with another would silently present an empty design. So identity has to live where the provenance stamp already lives (the sidecar beside the store), be written once at creation, and be REFUSED rather than defaulted when a later open disagrees with it — the same shape as the schema stamp refusing a graph a binary cannot read in full. Two consequences follow. Identity must be stable across machines, or the same design mirrored from two places reads as two designs; and it must be distinct by default, since two projects both called the design's default name would mirror into each other and the collision guard would report every node as a clash. This is rule:no-foreclosure item 5 arriving as real work rather than as a hypothetical.

properties.name: Someone without the repo can reach a design, read it, and contribute to it
properties.statement: Anthony and his brother work on each other's ideas from opposite coasts, and today the only way to reach a design is to clone the repository that carries it. The intent is that a design can be made reachable to a named collaborator without handing them the code: they can read what it says, ask it questions, and contribute intent back — the collaboration is on the DESIGN, which is often the part a second person can help with before they know anything about the implementation. Two things this must not become. It must not make the design's home ambiguous: whatever hosts a shared copy, the repo file stays the durable record, or a hosting outage becomes a design outage (req:persistence, dec:repo-file-embedded). And it must not silently widen who can write: reaching a design is not the same as authoring in it, so a contribution must be attributable to a person (the Contributor layer, which exists) and the reach must be granted rather than assumed. Whether this is served by git remotes that already span both coasts, by a hosted service, or by both, is the open question recorded as dec:central-host — this requirement states the need, not the machinery.

properties.name: Where a design admits it, design its simulator too — and test there first
properties.statement: A design usually has to operate in an environment. Where it is reasonable to build a simulated version of that environment — or a digital twin of the design itself — reflow2 should treat THE SIMULATOR AS SOMETHING TO BE DESIGNED, not as an implementation detail that appears later, and should support a progression: exercise the design in simulation first, iron out what that reveals, then move to progressively more realistic tests and only then to real fielding. The payoff is risk removed before it is expensive: an issue found in simulation costs a rebuild, the same issue found in the field costs a deployment and sometimes a system. THE CAVEAT IS PART OF THE REQUIREMENT, not a footnote — not every design admits a meaningful simulation, and a tool that insisted on one would produce elaborate fictions for the designs that do not. So the first question is whether a simulator is feasible and worth it for THIS design, asked rather than assumed, and a design that answers no must be able to say so on the record without being nagged.

properties.name: The core is deterministic and LLM-free
properties.statement: The runtime core must be free of LLM and provider dependencies and neutral to the interaction surface; LLM reasoning enters only behind a sync, object-safe seam.

properties.name: Drift is reported with its direction and its meaning, not just its magnitude
properties.statement: When the design and the build diverge, reflow2 must say which way and about what — not merely that a file's contents moved. Three things follow. Direction: a system that has grown capability the design never recorded is a different condition from one whose design overstates it, and today both arrive as an identical checksum change, so understatement is invisible exactly where it is largest. Meaning: the report must say what the design now claims wrongly, because asking someone to decide whether the design still holds while telling them only that bytes changed puts the entire burden of finding the delta on the person least likely to have time for it — which is how the design goes stale despite a mechanism designed to stop it. And write-back: where the design was recovered from documents, bringing the design up to date must be able to reach those documents, or the source everyone actually reads stays wrong while the graph quietly becomes right.

properties.name: The driving agents are coding agents, not humans
properties.statement: The primary consumers are Claude Code and grok build (plus OpenCode/Copilot), which reach the system as MCP tools plus an installed skill kit. The human is reached only through the agent.

properties.name: An epoch can be planned, not only recorded
properties.statement: The temporal axis must run forward as well as back, in TWO PAIRED VIEWS of the same architecture (Anthony, 2026-07-28: 'in systems engineering, I think this would be 2 views of the same system'): increments in TIME — epochs, what the architecture is expected to be at epoch_1..n — and increments in CAPABILITY — what each small, frequent release adds, the release-fast-in-small-increments practice now common in industry (his brother's project ships ~2 minor releases a week). Both views must exist, each comparable as a delta: any two epochs, any two increments, or either against the present. With many moving parts — an ecosystem of coupled repos, each with its own graph — an epoch or increment must pin the set of per-repo design versions it means, or the question 'which epoch are we talking about?' has no answer, which is the failure this exists to prevent. Original idea 2026-07-28 ('epoch branches: project_x:epoch_1 captures what we expect the graph to look like at epoch_1'), amended the same day with the two-views framing. THE ATOM, Anthony's distillation 2026-07-28: the roadmap is a SATISFACTION SCHEDULE — a mapping of requirements to the epoch or increment where they are satisfied: 'in epoch 1, requirements A and B are satisfied; in increment 3, requirements C, D and E are expected to be satisfied; in epoch 27, KPP 1 is required to be satisfied.' His own verbs carry the three modalities the mapping must distinguish: ARE satisfied (recorded history — the backward direction the graph already does), EXPECTED to be satisfied (a plan, carrying confidence that decays with horizon per req:plans-move-honestly), and REQUIRED to be satisfied by (an obligation whose miss at arrival is a computed violation, the scheduling face of a KPP — content inviolability from req:inviolable-intent gains a deadline dimension).

properties.name: reflow2 explains what it is and how to run it before it explains what it believes
properties.statement: Someone arriving at reflow2 cold must learn, in plain language and before any philosophy, what it physically is and how it runs on their machine: a binary they run locally, a design graph kept as a file in their own repository, and a coding agent that talks to it over MCP. They must then find where the agent instructions go and two or three concrete uses — starting a design from nothing, recovering one from a system that already exists, and asking what breaks if something changes. The doctrine that makes reflow2 worth using is not the entry point to it.

properties.name: Install is one command, update is one word
properties.statement: A consumer installs reflow2 with a single command from a stable public URL (curl | bash or the platform equivalent) and updates with a single short command; releases are frequent and very minor, so updating is routine and cheap rather than an event. Modeled on the Claude Code installer/update experience the user named as the target (2026-07-20).

properties.name: Every artifact traces to the intent it serves
properties.statement: Traceability runs from concept through operations without a break.

properties.name: The graph can catch up after unrecorded change
properties.statement: When work arrives from elsewhere — a git pull bringing commits made on another machine or by a session that never touched this machine's live store — the design must be able to catch up on demand, in two layers. LAYER 1, THE RECORD: a machine's live store is a long-lived cache of the committed export (req:stale-seat-knows states the write-side guard; this is the read side). After a pull, the store must take on the pulled record's changes: fast-forward when only the record moved, three-way merge (base = the last export both sides share, from git history) when both moved — never a blind overwrite in either direction. LAYER 2, THE CODE: commits in the pull that changed the project without updating the graph must then be walked against the synced graph through the ordinary two-sided drift questions. Catching up is an interrogation, never a bulk import: the graph re-earns coherence, it does not absorb whatever happened. Anthony's scenario, 2026-07-28 (amending his first wording of today): 'I have been working reflow2 from a home computer mostly; I'm doing this in another session on a different computer. When I get home I'd like to git pull the latest, then run delta and it should reconcile any deltas with what it had. I often don't restart the claude code session at home, so the graph it has will be in whatever state I left it.'

properties.name: The graph is the index of its own snapshots
properties.statement: Git already stores versions, tags, branches and releases well, and reflow2 must not duplicate that. What reflow2 must own is the MAP: the graph tracks its own snapshots — which epoch_n or increment_n a thing belongs to, and where that snapshot lives (the git ref) — so a user asks the graph and never has to remember which branch holds which epoch. Anthony, 2026-07-28: 'what does this mean for reflow2 when most of what I discussed is what git already does? I think the answer is that the graph should track the snapshots (it is one graph in time) and therefore which epoch_n or increment_n something is. A user shouldn't have to remember which git branch a particular epoch or increment is in.' The in-repo precedent already exists for the backward direction: rel:v0180 lives in the graph, tag v0.18.0 lives in git, and the graph node names the version — nobody greps tags to learn what shipped. This requirement extends that same division of labor forward.

properties.name: Gaps become questions, not guesses
properties.statement: Where the design is underspecified, the system must ask the human in plain language and record the answer, rather than silently choosing a default.

properties.name: The past is never overwritten
properties.statement: Updating the design to match the build must not erase what was intended.

properties.name: A published interface carries enough to check compatibility, not just prose
properties.statement: When a design publishes an Interface, the published spec must carry the things two systems actually have to agree on, in a form a computation can compare — not a free-text blob a human has to read. The user's six characteristics: (1) ARCHITECTURAL STYLE AND PROTOCOL — the technology (REST, gRPC, GraphQL, WebSockets; RS-232, PCIe, CAN bus) and the communication paradigm, synchronous request-response versus asynchronous event-driven; (2) DATA STRUCTURE AND TYPES — payload serialization (JSON, XML, protobuf, raw binary) and a schema saying which fields are mandatory, their types, and their formatting constraints; (3) OPERATIONS AND ENDPOINTS — where to send a request (URL, port, memory address, function name) and what actions are permitted (HTTP verbs, RPC methods, read/write commands); (4) AUTHENTICATION AND SECURITY — how identity is verified (API keys, OAuth2, TLS certificates, cryptographic signatures) and how data is protected in transit and at rest; (5) ERROR HANDLING AND STATE CODES — the status vocabulary and a consistent failure structure the consumer can parse automatically; (6) PERFORMANCE AND CONSTRAINTS — rate limits, throttling, maximum concurrency, and timeout thresholds. THE POINT IS NOT COMPLETENESS FOR ITS OWN SAKE: it is that two designs cannot be checked for INCOMPATIBILITY at their seam unless the seam is described in comparable terms. Today reflow2 structures roughly one and a half of these six (medium, and designation) and puts the rest into one free-text `spec` string or nowhere at all — so mirror_surface can link two designs and still not tell you they disagree.

properties.name: Intent that must hold no matter what is recorded as inviolable, and a violation is computed, not remembered
properties.statement: A design must be able to record intent that no downstream decision may trade away — a key performance parameter, in the acquisition sense: a threshold that, if missed, fails the effort regardless of how well everything else went. Inviolable intent is distinct from a Requirement (a goal to achieve, tradeable against other goals) and from a Constraint (a limit imposed on the design). reflow2 must (a) let that intent be stated with its threshold and, where it applies, its objective value; (b) COMPUTE a violation rather than rely on anyone remembering — an accepted Decision, an allocation, or a change whose blast radius contradicts a KPP must be surfaced loudly and above ordinary gaps; and (c) show a KPP crossing in impact analysis BEFORE the edit is made, not after it has been committed. A KPP that nothing checks is a comment.

properties.name: Invoked as an MCP server over stdio
properties.statement: The user-facing surface is the reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio, installed into a consumer project by tools/reflow2_init.py, which merges rather than overwrites existing agent configuration.

properties.name: The design says which interfaces are the published boundaries, and computations read that distinction
properties.statement: Some interfaces are the boundary a system is known by; most are internal plumbing. The design must be able to say which — and the distinction must earn its keep by being read, not merely stored (dec:edge-orthogonality). From the MOSA guidebook Anthony supplied (OUSD(R&E), February 2025), whose entire discipline turns on designating modular system interfaces and then holding them stable and open, and independently from BL-45's system-of-systems thread, which found the same hole from the other side: nothing marks an Interface external-facing, so "visible to others" versus "mine to change" is undeclarable. Two independent routes to one missing property. What must read it, or the designation is decoration: a change that crosses a published boundary is a different risk from one that stays behind it, and impact analysis should say which it is BEFORE the edit; a design that publishes a surface should be able to export exactly that surface and nothing internal; and a composed design (req:design-composes) links through published boundaries, never through another system's internals. What this must NOT become: an assertion that a boundary is stable. Whether a published interface has in fact held is a matter of evidence — its drift history — not a property anyone sets.

properties.name: The install must land its pointer where the agent will actually read it
properties.statement:
FOUND IN USE, 2026-07-28: Anthony installed the kit into dynograph-foundation, opened a session there, reconnected the MCP server, and reported that no reflow2 skills appeared. The server was healthy and holding the graph. The kit was invisible.

THE CAUSE, and it is the SAME DEFECT CLASS `reflow2_init.py` already documents having been bitten by, in the opposite direction. `INSTRUCTION_FILES` adds a pointer line to every instruction-file convention THAT ALREADY EXISTS, and creates `AGENTS.md` when the project owns no such file. dynograph-foundation had neither `AGENTS.md` nor `CLAUDE.md`, so a fresh `AGENTS.md` was written — correct by the agents.md convention, and not the file Claude Code reads first. The installer's own comment records the storyflow case: "storyflow carries CLAUDE.md and no AGENTS.md, so the installer saw nothing to protect, wrote a fresh AGENTS.md, and left the file Claude Code actually reads with no mention of reflow2 — the whole kit invisible on the primary path." That fix protected an existing `CLAUDE.md`. It did not cover a project that has NO instruction file at all, which is the ordinary state of a repo that has never been agent-worked.

SO THE RULE IS NOT "protect what exists" BUT "reach what reads". A greenfield or never-agent-worked repo is the common case for adopt, and it is exactly the case where the installer currently produces a file the primary harness may never open.

THE SECOND HALF, which the same session surfaced: the SKILLS ARE SERVED and correctly so, but the eight slash commands that make them usable (`/gaps`, `/health`, `/where`, `/req`, `/decisions`, `/debt`, `/brainstorm`, `/kpp`) live only in reflow2's own `.claude/commands/` and ship in no kit. So every consumer project loses the ergonomics, and a user who has worked in reflow2's repo experiences the consumer install as broken rather than as thin. The commands are pure pointers — each says "use skill X" and hardcodes no path — so they do not carry the staleness that `dec:skills-served` was written to prevent. Whether to ship them is nonetheless a decision that touches that decision's reasoning, and is Anthony's to make rather than mine.

WHAT "INSTALLED CORRECTLY" HAS TO MEAN. Not "the files were written" — the install reported success in the failing case. It has to mean the agent, in a fresh session, is told reflow2 exists on the path its own harness actually reads.

properties.name: One reflow2 can hold several designs, and a session says which one it is working on
properties.statement: A person works on more than one project at a time, so reflow2 must be able to hold more than one design without their contents mixing, and a session must state which design it is operating on before it can read or write. Anthony, 2026-07-25: he has reflow2 itself and storyflow; his brother has several. Three properties follow. Selection is EXPLICIT — a session that has not named its design must be refused rather than defaulted to the last one used or the only one present, because a tool call landing in the wrong project is a silent corruption that no gap detector would ever notice. Segregation is enforced by the store, not by convention: every node and edge already carries a graph_id, which is exactly the primitive this needs, and today it is pinned to the constant "reflow2" — so the mechanism exists and is unused, the same shape as the temporal axis and the inviolable-intent vocabulary before them. And the identity of a design must be stable across machines, so the same project reached from two places is one design rather than two that happen to share a name. This is deliberately silent on where the designs live: one process per design and one holding many are both answers to it, and that is the hosting question, not this requirement.

properties.name: Modularity is computed from the design, not asserted by the architecture diagram
properties.statement: A design that calls something a module must be able to be CHECKED on it. From the MOSA guidebook's conformance criteria (Table D-1: "demonstrate severable modular components"; components "encapsulated, cohesive, loosely coupled"), reframed to reflow2's own rule that a claim is derived from evidence rather than set by hand — the same move already made for requirement certainty and for delivery. The operative test is severability, and reflow2 already owns the machinery: if the blast radius of a change inside a part stops at that part's published boundaries, the part is severable; if it leaks past them, the part is not modular whatever the diagram says. Cohesion and coupling are already computed (community structure, the modularity score, the god-component finding) — the gap is severability, which needs req:key-interfaces to know where a boundary is. Two guards. This reports, never scores: a coarse-but-honest module is not a defect, and a single opaque part legitimately encapsulates everything beneath it (dec:report-dont-judge). And the vocabulary stays neutral (req:design-anything) — the acquisition community's words for these criteria belong in a VIEW over the computation, never in the schema, or reflow2 will have adopted one domain's language as its own.

properties.name: A session that has no design graph is told so, in band
properties.statement: When reflow2 cannot open the graph — another session holds the single-writer lock, or the graph was stamped by a different reflow2 — the MCP server must still complete the handshake and carry the reason where the agent will read it. Exiting at startup makes the outage indistinguishable from "reflow2 was never configured for this project", and an agent that concludes that skips the design-first process for a reason nobody recorded. Field-reported by the StoryFlow fleet, 2026-07-25.

properties.name: The user never needs systems engineering
properties.statement: The graph carries the discipline; the user answers plain questions.

properties.name: Setting up a project is not a step — reflow2 is installed once per machine
properties.statement:
FROM ANTHONY, 2026-07-28, twice in one session and the second time as scope: "we need to make this as easy as possible. it is getting too hard to just start a project and then there are multiple steps after just to get it working" — and then, decisively: "my brother is using reflow2 on his machine. I'm using it another machine and this machine to develop it and use it. this isn't a fix for just this machine - it is a fix to make this easy for all users that ever use reflow2 from now on."

WHAT HE HAD MEASURED, on a real project (brainmaker) minutes before saying it: install the binary, run a per-project installer naming an absolute path into a reflow2 checkout, restart the agent, then type a slash command that had never shipped. Four steps to reach the first design action, three of them after the install, and the last one failed.

THE OBSERVATION THAT MAKES IT SOLVABLE: none of reflow2's per-project footprint is per-project in NATURE. `--graph-path .reflow2/graph` is relative to the working directory, so ONE registration still gives every project its own graph. The slash commands are pointers at served skills, so one global copy carries nothing that can go stale. The loop hooks are the same script in every project. What is genuinely per-repo is only the committed design export, and a pointer file for a repo whose OTHER contributors' agents must be told reflow2 governs it.

SO THE REQUIREMENT IS: after a one-time machine install, a user starts designing any project by opening their agent in a directory and asking — no installer, no config, no restart, no per-project step of any kind. Setup that survives per project is a defect, not a feature.

THE COUNTERWEIGHT, and it is what makes this honest rather than merely convenient: a machine-wide install must cost a directory that will never be designed exactly NOTHING. No graph created, no hook output, no state written. Most directories on a machine should stay untouched, and they must stay untouched by construction rather than by the user avoiding them.

properties.name: No silent fallbacks or drops
properties.statement: Failures and skipped work are surfaced loudly, never swallowed.

properties.name: The loop nudge covers the session that never touches the graph
properties.statement: A session that edits code while making zero reflow2 calls must receive the same one-time Stop nudge as one that writes the graph unchecked: the nudge arms on the harness's file-edit events (Edit/Write), not only on reflow2 write events. Today loop_nudge.py counts only mcp__reflow2__ writes, so the total-bypass session — the agent that ignores the design brain entirely — passes the Stop hook silently. Constraints carried over: the hook never reads the graph (single-writer lock), blocks once and never twice, and names what is owed (loop_status; impact-check before further edits, link-artifacts after) rather than demanding a ritual call; an edit-count threshold bounds false positives on typo/docs sessions. (BL-90, BL-74 family.)

properties.name: The path the coherence loop relies on to interrupt an agent is proven to interrupt one
properties.statement: The Stop-hook nudge and the read-side loop_hint are the only mechanisms that make the loop self-correcting, and nothing proves they reach a live agent: the existing suite tests the nudge script given its inputs, not that the hook is installed and fires. Prove the path end to end in a real session, and give it a backstop for when it is absent — a mechanism relied on to interrupt you is worthless until observed doing so.

properties.name: Someone who did not build the system can be told where a new piece of work belongs
properties.statement: A person inheriting a mature design must be able to ask "we need to add this — where does it go?" and be answered from the graph: which existing part should own it, what the change would touch, which decisions already govern that area and must not be casually contradicted, what intent it must not break, and who authored the reasoning so they can be asked. Answering "what is this system and what has been decided" is necessary but not sufficient; the requirement is satisfied only when the second question — where and how do I add to it — is also answered, and when the answer says honestly which parts of the real system the design does not cover.

properties.name: The design persists in-repo alongside the code
properties.statement: The graph lives at ./.reflow2/graph inside the consumer project, so the design travels with the repo; export/import is deterministic so a backup under git shows what actually changed.

properties.name: A plan is a dated claim whose movement is on the record
properties.statement: A planned epoch or increment is a claim about the future, and its reliability decays with horizon — Anthony, 2026-07-28: 'the further out you plan your epochs, the more volatile they are, almost like what the Black-Scholes model was created for. There will always be a delta between what was planned for a particular epoch and what was actually delivered when we arrive at it.' Three obligations follow. (1) A planned claim carries its confidence, and far claims carry less — the ANTICIPATES edge's existing confidence property (0.0-1.0) is the vocabulary hook. (2) Arriving at an epoch produces the planned-vs-delivered delta as a matter of course, and REPLANNING IS RECORDED: when a planned epoch's content moves, the plan's own change is a dated event on the record, so 'what did we believe at the time?' stays answerable — the same axis-Z discipline the as-built record already gets. (3) Firmness is two-dimensional and the dimensions move independently: a KPP (req:inviolable-intent, cap:kpp) is inviolable in CONTENT — it cannot be weakened to make a plan work — but may SLIP IN TIME to a later increment or epoch, and the slip is a recorded dated event, never a silent re-pin; ordinary requirements may flex in both content and time as factors affect the project. Evidence for the open dec:plan-time-axis question of whether scheduled time becomes a first-class axis. PARTIAL SATISFACTION AT ARRIVAL (Anthony, 2026-07-28, raised as a nuance, not decided): 'what happens if a requirement is only partially satisfied? Does the part that was not satisfied get transferred to the following epoch/increment, or is it discontinued?' The candidate mechanism is already in the design: a partially-met requirement is DECOMPOSED (req:requirement-lineage — the split is on the record, both children knowing their parent), the satisfied child closes at this epoch, and the remainder's fate is the one question that must be ASKED, never defaulted: transferred (re-pinned to a later epoch, a recorded slip) or discontinued (retire-from-design's discipline — dropped on the user's word, with the reason). The status vocabulary already carries both answers (deferred / dropped). He expects further nuances of arrival semantics; the modalities and rules here are an open list, not a closed one.

properties.name: Runs on Linux and macOS developer machines
properties.statement: Target platforms are Linux and macOS. Consumers must not pay a RocksDB C++ rebuild for a routine reflow2 update; the core runs on an in-memory backend with RocksDB opt-in.

properties.name: A proposed change can be read as a delta before it lands
properties.statement: A pull request is a delta that has not happened yet. For a project under design control, the design must be able to read a candidate change (a PR branch, a patch) the same way delta reads a landed one — which artifacts would drift, and which capabilities, interfaces and requirements those artifacts realize (propagate from the touched set) — but STRICTLY READ-ONLY: a review reports what the change would mean to the design and never writes an accept, because accepts record what IS, and a PR is not yet. When the PR touches a published or consumed interface, the report must say so by name, because that is the part of the diff a reviewer cannot see from the code alone. Anthony's scenario, 2026-07-28: at his job (a founding site of the Bluesky project, blueskyproject.io), 'just today I got a request to review a PR on bluesky-httpserver — delta would see the difference between the current version and what the PR adds/changes.' The cross-repo half of his scenario — bluesky-httpserver is tightly coupled with bluesky-queueserver; does the PR affect the other repo? — is deliberately NOT this requirement: it is the standing composition thread (req:seam-incompatibility, req:composed-analysis, dec:linked-repos-poc), where the delta review's touched-interface list becomes the input to a seam check against the coupled design's mirrored surface.

properties.name: A published surface must be able to carry a behavioural promise, not only structure
properties.statement:
FOUND BY A REAL TRIAL, 2026-07-28, and it is reflow2's defect rather than either project's: the dynograph-foundation session, publishing its offer to the reflow2 session, could not express the one commitment its consumer most needed.

THE MECHANISM, exactly. `export_surface` emits published Interfaces, the Components either side of them, and the contract artifacts. It withholds everything else as internal — including every Requirement, deliberately, because a consumer has no business reading its dependency's internal intent. But BEHAVIOURAL COMMITMENTS LIVE IN REQUIREMENTS. So the document reflow2 offers as "the published surface" carries structure and no promises, and there is no way to publish one.

THE CONCRETE CASE. reflow2's own Cargo.toml asserts, in a comment, that dynograph's `open_rocksdb` "fails loud (foundation contract), rather than silently falling back to memory". That is a real, load-bearing promise — a silent fallback to an in-memory store would lose a consumer's data with no error. dynograph's graph HAS it, as an accepted Requirement ("A build without RocksDB must work, and must fail loud rather than fall back"). The provider holds the promise, the consumer depends on the promise, and the surface export cannot carry it between them. So it lives where it is useless: a prose comment in the consumer's build file, on the wrong side of the seam, where the provider will never see it change.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN A MISSING FEATURE. A published surface that structurally cannot contain half of what a published surface is for will be *believed* — it says "published surface" on the tin, it counts what it withheld, and it looks complete. A consumer reading it concludes the provider promises nothing behavioural, when in fact the provider promises plenty and simply cannot say so.

TWO WAYS OUT, and they are not equal. (1) A prose companion document alongside the export — cheap, and it sits outside every check reflow2 has, so it drifts exactly like `docs/endpoints.md` did in the provider's own repo. (2) A `designation` on Requirement, the way Interface already carries one, so a behavioural promise can be marked publishable and travel with the surface — the export machinery, the withholding count, and the drift checks all then apply to it unchanged. Option 2 is the recommendation: it reuses the mechanism whose semantics are already settled (`internal` by default, because publishing is a commitment nobody should make by accident) rather than inventing a second, unchecked channel.

NOT A LICENCE TO PUBLISH REQUIREMENTS WHOLESALE. Most requirements are internal intent and must stay withheld. The designation is opt-in per requirement, exactly as it is per interface, and the default stays `internal`.

properties.name: A read reminds the agent of loop debt at the moment of attention
properties.statement: The agent should be reminded of outstanding coherence-loop debt while it is looking at the graph mid-session — not only at SessionStart (fires once) and Stop (fires at the very end). Reads (scan_nodes, get_node, search_design, graph_report, …) are the agent's first and most frequent action, so a read that returns while the loop is owed something is a well-timed place to surface it, closing the gap between the two existing triggers. This is the read-side sibling of the write tools' loop_hint and a member of the BL-74 "fire on a trigger, not on virtue" family: the reminder must ride a call the agent already makes, so remembering reflow2 does not depend on the agent's discipline under operational load.

properties.name: Reading the design does not require owning it
properties.statement: A session that cannot take the write lock should still be able to READ the design — orientation, detectors, reports — rather than having no design brain at all. RocksDB supports this (open_for_read_only, open_as_secondary) but dynograph-storage does not expose it, so this needs an upstream change to a tag-pinned dependency. Six concurrent sessions on one machine is the actual working pattern, and today five of them get nothing.

properties.name: Released equals designed
properties.statement: At release the design must describe what was actually released.

properties.name: A requirement knows where it came from: stated, decomposed from a parent, or derived from a decision
properties.statement: Requirements multiply in two different ways and reflow2 must tell them apart, because they behave differently. An ORIGINAL requirement is the stakeholder's own word. A DECOMPOSED requirement is a 1:1 split of a parent into smaller testable pieces, adding no new information — so satisfying every child satisfies the parent, and a parent's delivery is therefore derivable from its children rather than needing its own capability. A DERIVED requirement is new technical necessity that nobody asked for, created because of a design decision — so it traces to that DECISION, not to a parent goal, and if the decision is ever re-opened the derived requirement may cease to have any reason to exist. Three consequences follow. Delivery must roll up a decomposition tree instead of treating every requirement as an independent leaf. Re-opening a decision must be able to say which requirements existed only because of the road taken. And the distinction must survive the loss of the person who made it: an original requirement is the only kind whose loss loses intent, because decomposed and derived ones can be regenerated from what they came from, and that is precisely why the link back must be recorded rather than remembered.

properties.name: The open structural-defect list means still-needs-attention
properties.statement: A structural defect that has been reviewed and consciously accepted must move out of the open list into a reviewed one — not deleted, not hidden — the way an acknowledged gap already does. Found as friction 2026-07-25: detect_defects reports the same six findings every run, all six carrying recorded Decisions explaining why they stand, so a genuine seventh would arrive into a list nobody reads carefully and the count is the only signal. reviewed_gaps already keeps this promise for gaps on the stated grounds that "a list that can never reach zero gets skimmed"; the defect side makes the same promise in its docs and does not keep it. Two properties carried over from the gap side: the acceptance records WHY, as a real node that outlives the session, and it expires when the affected nodes change, so an accepted defect comes back for a fresh look rather than staying quietly accepted forever.

properties.name: The roads not taken are preserved and forkable
properties.statement: reflow2 preserves not only what was decided but what was considered and rejected: every Decision keeps its unchosen alternatives as first-class, forkable siblings, and any past decision can be re-opened at its epoch and a different branch taken from that point. The design is a navigable decision tree, not only a linear history — the extension of req:intent-preserved from 'the past is never overwritten' to 'the roads not taken are never lost either.' The unchosen option and its rationale are stored; the alternative's consequence design is computed on demand by replay, never eagerly maintained.

properties.name: When two linked designs disagree at a seam, say so
properties.statement:
NOW ANSWERED BY MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN ARGUMENT (trial against dynograph-foundation, 2026-07-28). The open question was whether `compose_and_analyse` plus the ordinary detectors is enough, or whether a dedicated incompatibility check is needed. It is not enough, and the trial shows exactly where the line falls.

WHAT WAS RUN. dynograph-foundation published its offer (`docs/published-surface.json`, 15 boundaries: 11 library, 3 REST, 1 data). reflow2 composed against it in a throwaway graph seeded from its own committed export. Their 31 nodes and 61 edges imported with ZERO skipped edges.

ROUND ONE, before any matching: 0 seam findings, and one loud structural signal — "29 nodes form a cluster disconnected from the rest of the design". That is the detector correctly reporting that two designs were placed side by side and nothing joined them. Useful, and exactly right.

ROUND TWO, after drawing seven CONSUMES edges by hand from reflow2's components to their published boundaries (store→storage-api and core-api, schema→schema-doc, search→text-api, ingest→resolution-api, heal→graph-api, dimensions→vector-api): the disconnected-cluster finding DISAPPEARED, and the seam produced **zero findings of any kind**. What remained were two findings wholly inside the provider's design.

WHAT THAT PROVES. Composition plus the ordinary detectors checks CONNECTIVITY, not COMPATIBILITY. The existing detectors reason about structure — missing intent, unsatisfied requirements, orphans, cycles, single points of failure — and a well-formed seam trips none of them. But a contract mismatch is a comparison of PROPERTIES ACROSS A PAIR of interfaces: my expected payload format against theirs, my required auth against theirs, my assumed paradigm against theirs, a behavioural promise against its absence. No ordinary detector compares two nodes' properties against each other, so no ordinary detector can ever produce that finding. The silence was not the absence of problems; it was the absence of anyone looking.

THE SECOND HALF, and it is worse. The seven seam edges were HAND-ASSERTED and nothing checked them. I claimed `cmp:store` consumes `dynograph::ifc:storage-api` and the graph accepted it without question. A WRONG hand-match produces exactly the same clean result as a right one — so today the seam analysis is only as good as the assertion nobody verified. That is `req:complementary-pairing`'s job on the matching side, and this requirement's job on the terms side.

WHAT IT MUST CHECK, from the properties `req:interface-spec-complete` already put on Interface: `paradigm` (a consumer written for request-response cannot be pointed at an event feed), `payload_format` (protobuf against JSON fails immediately and totally), `auth` and `transport_security` (the consumer that assumed `none` gets 401s in production; a provider offering `none` against a consumer requiring `tls` is a refusal to connect), `operations` (calling an operation the provider does not offer), `error_model`, and `payload_schema`. Plus the behavioural terms that `req:publishable-promise` would let a surface carry at all.

REPORT, DO NOT JUDGE. A mismatch is a finding to put to the two sides, not a verdict — `unspecified` on either side is an unknown, not a conflict, and must read as "nobody has said" rather than as agreement. The false-green rule from the trial applies here too: silence must never be reported as compatibility.

properties.name: Who is working is a property of the session, not of the server process
properties.statement: Seat identity is currently minted once per process, which is correct while one session owns one server and wrong the moment several sessions share one. A hosted server would report the same seat for every client, so every claim would carry the same owner and claim_report's liveness would answer a question nobody asked — the mechanism would look like it worked while telling all six sessions they are each other. The seat must come from the client: the transport already assigns a session id with zero coordination, which is exactly what dec:identity-out-of-band says a name should be. The read-side loop_hint's fire-on-change throttle has the same shape of bug — it is per-service state, so a hint earned by one session lands on whichever session reads next.

properties.name: What a session learns is written to the graph as it is learned, not summarized into a file on the way out
properties.statement: A working session produces decisions, findings and realizations, and those are design content: they belong in the graph, recorded at the moment they occur, so a later session can query them rather than read a narrative. Two properties follow. First, capture is incremental — a summary written at the end is the one a busy session never gets to, and an end-of-session digest is a retelling rather than a record. Second, the enforcement must point at the graph: whatever mechanism insists a session leave its takeaways behind must be satisfiable only by graph writes, never by touching a prose file, or the prose file becomes the memory and the graph becomes decoration. The agent must then be able to ask its own history — what was decided about X, when, by whom, and against what state of the design — using the same query surface a person uses.

properties.name: A session on another machine works the same design, live
properties.statement: Sessions running on a DIFFERENT machine must be able to work the same design at the same time, through the same one server, without exporting, merging or pulling. The third of the three cases: different projects on one machine has always worked; several sessions on one machine works through --http; this is the one where the seats are not on the same box. Because there is no authentication, being reachable off the machine must be a deliberate act — the server answers only for hosts that were named on the command line, and says so when a bind would otherwise fail silently.

properties.name: Several sessions on one machine work the same design at the same time
properties.statement: Anthony, 2026-07-26: "I want to have multiple sessions running and being able to use the same reflow2 graph." Six concurrent sessions must read and write ONE design concurrently, without a worktree each and without an export-and-merge round trip between them. The store is single-writer per process, so this is served by one server process holding the graph with many client sessions connected — there is still exactly one writer. Reads must not queue behind each other (the graph sits behind a lock that today serialises everything), each client must be its own seat, and a client must never be able to see a partial write.

properties.name: A seat learns the shared design moved before it writes over it
properties.statement: A session's live graph is a long-lived cache of the committed design export. Before that session writes the export back, reflow2 must tell it that the committed record has moved since it last synced — the way git refuses a non-fast-forward push rather than silently winning. A stale export is not a conflicting export, it is a complete one, so the merge driver merges it cleanly and the other seat's work disappears without a conflict marker.

properties.name: A property the detector ignores is a property that lies
properties.statement:
FOUND BY USING THE GRAPH, 2026-07-28, and the third defect this week that inspection had not found and one real use did.

WHAT HAPPENED. Anthony decided the slash commands should ship with the kit, which QUALIFIES `dec:skills-served` rather than overturning it — same reasoning, narrower scope. The schema has carried the vocabulary for that relationship from the beginning: CONTRADICTS is documented as "two decisions/requirements/claims that conflict (OR, WITH alignment=supporting, REINFORCE)". So the corroboration was recorded exactly as prescribed, with `alignment: supporting` — and `detect_defects` reported a structural defect, because the contradiction loop read the edge TYPE and never looked at the property.

WHY THE NOISE WAS NOT THE DAMAGE. The damage was that both ways out were wrong. Acknowledge it, and a defect that is not one enters `reviewed_defects` as if a judgement had been made. Stop drawing the edge, and the design silently loses the fact that one decision qualifies another — which is precisely the kind of reasoning a design graph exists to keep. And an open list that can never reach zero gets SKIMMED, which is the failure the whole detect-and-ask discipline is built to prevent.

THE GENERAL RULE, worth stating beyond this instance: A SCHEMA PROPERTY THAT NO COMPUTATION READS IS A PROPERTY THAT LIES. It invites people to record something true, and then behaves as though they had not. reflow2 has now been bitten by this shape three times in two days — `orphan_node` ignoring DOCUMENTS so a well-documented artifact reads as loose; `export_surface` withholding every Requirement so a published promise could not travel; and this. Each was a value the schema offered and no detector consulted.

WHAT THE FIX MUST NOT DO, and this is the load-bearing half: it must not silence the detector. An `opposing` edge is still a contradiction, and an edge that says NOTHING is still a contradiction — silence is not a claim of support, and every design written before today keeps its meaning exactly. A fix that made real conflicts vanish would be far worse than the noise it removed, so both counterweights are pinned by tests rather than asserted in a comment.

properties.name: A design survives a reflow2 upgrade
properties.statement: An existing graph opens, or is refused loudly with what to do.

properties.name: After setup, a project never has to change again for reflow2 to move
properties.statement: Installing reflow2 into a project should put a paragraph in the agent instructions and a server address in the MCP config, and nothing else that ever needs refreshing. Upgrades belong to the reflow2 package: today `reflow2_init.py` copies fifteen skills into two directory trees plus AGENTS.md, so upgrading means re-running init and taking thirty-odd changed files into a repo that has nothing to do with reflow2's release. Anthony's brother, 2026-07-25: "you wouldn't need to change anything in your repo again and updates would be confined to the reflow package." The installer's own docstring already concedes the defect — "the kit is copied into your project, so it otherwise freezes at install time while reflow2 keeps moving" — and reflow2's own kit manifest sat four releases stale without anything noticing (ver:kit-manifest-agrees).

properties.name: Text that enters the graph from outside is neutralised at the boundary, and the neutralisation is reported
properties.statement: reflow2's standing rule — graph text is data, never instructions — is enforced today only by prose in the skills and the server handshake, which is a rule addressed to a well-behaved reader. The requirement is that the mechanical half exists: text arriving from outside the session's own author (prose read out of a codebase by INGEST, a design export imported from another machine or another person, and anything a hosted surface would accept) is neutralised of the characters that carry hidden instructions before any agent reads it — invisible and zero-width characters, bidirectional overrides that make text render as something other than what it says, Unicode tag characters that smuggle a payload past a human reviewer, and metadata hidden in code-fence info strings. Two properties reflow2 must add to the technique it borrows. The neutralisation must be REPORTED, not silent: a design whose statements were quietly rewritten on the way in is a design nobody can audit, and rule 6 forbids silent drops — so the count and the kind of what was stripped travel with the result. And it must not touch legitimate design content: an arrow, an emoji, a maths symbol or a non-Latin script is ordinary text in a design that may be about anything, so the filter is a named list of instruction-carrying characters rather than a whitelist of what looks familiar.

properties.name: A "verified" claim says how old the check behind it is
properties.statement: When a capability claims to be verified, the design must be able to say whether the check behind that claim is older than the code it covers. A passing check proves the paths it drives, and nothing more — so when a capability's meaning widens without its check widening, the old green tick keeps being reported as if nothing had changed. reflow2 already records everything needed to notice: Verification.last_run_at is written on every status set, and the confirmation ledger already dates the accepts that moved an artifact's baseline. Nothing reads the two together. Where the dates do not exist the answer must be "cannot tell", stated plainly — never silence, and never an assumption that the check is current.

properties.name: The design can say what to work on next, and why that and not something else
properties.statement: A person returning to the design must be able to ask "what is the most pressing thing to work on?" and get an answer computed from the design itself, with its reasoning visible — not a hand-maintained ordering in a file. The answer must rank an unmade decision ABOVE the work that waits on it, because being told to build something blocked on a choice only the human can make is worse than being told nothing. It must distinguish what is undecided from what is unbuilt from what is misshapen, since those need different actions from different people. And it must be a projection over the graph, never a stored list: a second place where priority lives is a second place for it to go stale, which is the failure the whole backlog-in-the-graph move exists to end.

properties.description: Derived from reflow2's own Cargo.toml, not hand-written. Bumped v0.11.0 -> v0.12.0 on 2026-07-28 for a stated reason rather than as housekeeping (AGENTS.md forbids the latter): v0.12.0 closes a type leak reflow2 was structurally exposed to — `search_fulltext` returned `dynograph_text::TextHit`, from a crate reflow2 never names and reaches only through an optional feature — and it makes the `rocksdb` and `fulltext` feature NAMES a committed contract upstream, which is exactly the reliance this declaration records. Verified before the tag existed by building this consumer against the provider's unreleased tree. MIGRATION CHECKED, not assumed: `keys.rs` and `backend.rs` are untouched between the tags, so a graph written by v0.11.0 reads identically.

properties.state: {"description":"The capture half of KPPs, and the half a person actually touches. Anthony, 2026-07-25: the user says \\\"the system should be able to perform X\\\"; the agent, acting as the systems-engineering SME the user is not required to be (req:no-se-knowledge), recognises the shape of inviolable intent and asks — that sounds like something that MUST be met, is it? — and the user confirms or declines. WHY THE AGENT MUST NOT DECIDE IT: criticality is a claim about consequence, not about wording. Whether missing a threshold FAILS THE EFFORT depends on mission, contract and money that the graph does not hold and the agent cannot see. An agent that promoted a requirement to KPP on its own would be asserting the user's stake in their own project, which is the same forgery dec:certainty-derived forbids for requirement status — and worse here, because a KPP outranks every ordinary gap and would drag the whole detector's ranking with it. So: the agent PROPOSES, the human DISPOSES, and nothing enters as a KPP without the user's word. WHAT THE AGENT CAN LEGITIMATELY NOTICE, and it is more than intuition. A statement carrying a unit-bearing threshold (500 miles, 3000 pounds, 500 milliseconds) is already shaped like a KPP and may simply be unmodelled — the quantity/limit/direction triple has somewhere to go. Language of necessity ('must', 'shall', 'no less than') against language of preference ('should', 'aims to') is a real signal in acquisition prose. And a requirement whose failure the user has elsewhere described as fatal is a candidate the graph itself can surface. THE QUESTION MUST CARRY THE CONSEQUENCE, not just the label: asking 'is this a KPP?' invites a shrug, whereas asking 'if the system missed this by ten percent, would the effort have failed?' is answerable by someone who has never heard the term — which is the test req:no-se-knowledge sets. On confirmation the agent sets category kpp, and should ask for the threshold and, where one exists, the objective; on decline it stays an ordinary Requirement and the offer is not repeated.
